PRR: Pattern-recognition receptor: a germline-encoded INNATE receptor (e.g. TLRs, NLRs, RLRs) that detects conserved microbial PAMPs and reports only non-self, never the species.
PAMP: Pathogen-associated molecular pattern: a conserved microbial structure (LPS, teichoic acid, mannose, viral RNA, CpG DNA) recognized by innate PRRs.
TLR: Toll-like receptor: a PRR that drives CYTOKINE signaling for inflammation; surface TLRs read membrane PAMPs, endosomal TLRs (3/7/8/9) read nucleic acids.
TLR4: Surface Toll-like receptor for LPS (gram-negative bacteria); needs LBP and CD14 to deliver LPS and MD2 to stabilize it on the TLR4 dimer. Found on macrophages, DCs, mast cells.
TLR7: Endosomal Toll-like receptor sensing viral RNA, prominent on plasmacytoid dendritic cells to drive type I interferon.
TLR9: Endosomal Toll-like receptor sensing CpG DNA, on plasmacytoid dendritic cells to drive type I interferon.
NLR: NOD-like receptor: cytoplasmic PRR (NOD1/NOD2) sensing intracellular peptidoglycan, signaling via RIPK2 to NF-kB.
NOD2: Cytoplasmic NLR sensing bacterial peptidoglycan; variants are associated with BOTH Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis (so it does not distinguish them).
RLR: RIG-I-like receptor: cytoplasmic PRR (RIG-I, MDA-5) sensing cytoplasmic viral RNA, activating IRF3 to drive type I interferon.
NLRP3: The inflammasome sensor that assembles to activate caspase-1; a GAIN-OF-FUNCTION NLRP3 mutation causes CAPS (recurrent fever, hives, joint pain).
inflammasome: Cytoplasmic complex (e.g. NLRP3) whose sole job is to activate caspase-1, which CLEAVES inactive pro-IL-1beta into active IL-1beta.
LPS: Lipopolysaccharide: the conserved outer-membrane PAMP of gram-negative bacteria; the ligand for TLR4 and the classic TI-1 (T-independent) B-cell stimulus.
LBP: LPS-binding protein: hands LPS to CD14 for delivery to the TLR4 complex.
CD14: Co-receptor that receives LPS from LBP and presents it to TLR4/MD2.
MD2: Accessory protein that stabilizes LPS on the TLR4 homodimer.
MyD88: Adaptor downstream of most TLRs; triggers the IKK to IkB to NF-kB cascade for cytokine transcription.
IKK: IkB kinase: phosphorylates IkB, marking it for degradation so NF-kB can enter the nucleus.
IkB: Inhibitor that holds NF-kB in the cytoplasm; corticosteroids act by RAISING IkB to block NF-kB.
NF-kB: Master pro-inflammatory transcription factor driving cytokine genes; blocked by glucocorticoids (which act via IkB).
NFAT: Calcium-dependent transcription factor; dephosphorylated by calcineurin to enter the nucleus. Frozen in the cytoplasm by cyclosporine/tacrolimus.
AP-1: Transcription factor (c-Fos + c-Jun) downstream of the RAS/MAPK arm; one of three arms converging on the IL-2 gene.
IRF3: Transcription factor activated by RLRs to drive type I interferon (antiviral state).
PKR: Interferon-induced kinase that phosphorylates eIF2 to HALT viral protein synthesis.
eIF2: Translation initiation factor; phosphorylated by PKR to shut down viral protein synthesis.
type I interferon: Antiviral cytokine (IFN-alpha/beta) inducing an antiviral state; made mainly by plasmacytoid dendritic cells (~80-90% during viral infection).
IFN-gamma: Th1/NK signature cytokine that polarizes M1 macrophages (ROS/RNS), raises MHC I, and maintains granulomas; antagonistic to IL-4.
TNF-alpha: Dominant endothelial-activating cytokine; LOCAL release is protective inflammation, SYSTEMIC release causes septic shock and DIC.
IL-1: Central acute-inflammation cytokine (with TNF) from LPS-activated macrophages; activates endothelium and drives fever.
IL-1beta: Made as inactive pro-IL-1beta and cleaved by inflammasome caspase-1; causes fever (PGE2 set-point change).
IL-2: T-cell growth factor driving clonal expansion and BCL survival proteins; the convergence point of NF-kB, NFAT, and AP-1. Mainly from CD4 cells.
IL-4: Th2-inducing/effector cytokine (signal 3 via GATA3); drives B-cell IgE switching and M2 macrophages; antagonistic to IFN-gamma.
IL-5: Th2 cytokine that recruits and activates EOSINOPHILS against helminths.
IL-6: Acute-phase driver (hepatocyte pentraxins, neutrophil output); produces metabolic heat distinct from IL-1beta fever. With TGF-beta drives Th17.
IL-7: Survival cytokine from bone-marrow stroma for early B/T development; loss of its receptor on failed rearrangement triggers apoptosis.
IL-7R: IL-7 receptor: the SURVIVAL marker; memory T cells keep it (long-lived), short-lived effectors lose it. Does NOT distinguish T_CM from T_EM.
IL-8: CXCL8, the neutrophil chemokine; an NF-kB cytokine.
IL-10: Anti-inflammatory cytokine (with TGF-beta) that terminates the acute inflammatory response.
IL-12: Macrophage-derived cytokine that is signal 3 for Th1 (via T-bet) and a key NK activator.
IL-13: Th2 cytokine that with IL-4 drives M2 polarization and worm expulsion; pathogenic in ulcerative colitis.
IL-17: Th17 effector cytokine that recruits and activates NEUTROPHILS against extracellular bacteria.
IL-21: TFH/Th17 cytokine; in Crohn disease converts B cells into granzyme-B+ cytotoxic B cells.
IL-22: Th17 cytokine that reinforces the barrier by inducing antimicrobial defensins and loosening tight junctions to flush pathogens.
IL-33: Alarmin that partially activates mast cells (full degranulation still needs IgE-FcepsilonRI cross-linking).
TGF-beta: Anti-inflammatory cytokine; alone favors FoxP3 Tregs, but with IL-6 yields Th17. Released by macrophages after clearing apoptotic cells (quiet funeral).
TSLP: Cytokine secreted by mTECs in Hassall's corpuscles, driving DCs to induce FoxP3+ regulatory T cells.
PGE2: Prostaglandin E2: the mediator by which IL-1beta resets the hypothalamic temperature SET-POINT to cause fever.
T-bet: Master transcription factor of the Th1 lineage (induced by IL-12).
GATA3: Master transcription factor of the Th2 lineage (induced by IL-4).
ROR-gamma-T: Master transcription factor of the Th17 lineage (induced by IL-6 + TGF-beta).
FoxP3: Master transcription factor and marker of regulatory T cells (Tregs); also defines them alongside CD25 and CTLA-4.
Th1: Helper subset targeting INTRACELLULAR pathogens; IFN-gamma drives M1 macrophage killing. Master TF T-bet.
Th2: Helper subset targeting PARASITIC WORMS; IL-4/IL-5/IL-13 arm IgE/eosinophils and drive expulsion. Master TF GATA3.
Th17: Helper subset targeting EXTRACELLULAR bacteria; IL-17 recruits neutrophils. Master TF ROR-gamma-T.
Treg: Regulatory T cell: FoxP3+ CD25+ CTLA-4+ suppressor with high-affinity self-TCR; ~10% of peripheral CD4 cells, and falling below that raises autoimmunity risk.
TFH: Follicular helper T cell: provides CD40L and cytokine help to B cells in the germinal center for class switching and affinity maturation.
MHC: Major histocompatibility complex (HLA in humans): the most polymorphic loci in the genome; presents peptide to T cells and is the dominant trigger of transplant rejection.
HLA: Human leukocyte antigen: the human MHC; HLA-A/B/C are class I, HLA-DP/DQ/DR are class II.
MHC class I: Peptide-presenting molecule on ALL nucleated cells; displays endogenous (cytosolic) peptide to CD8 T cells. Loaded via proteasome + TAP.
MHC class II: Peptide-presenting molecule restricted to APCs (DCs, macrophages, B cells); displays exogenous (vesicular) peptide to CD4 T cells. Loaded via cathepsins + HLA-DM.
MHC restriction: T cells recognize antigen ONLY when displayed on self-MHC; foreign MHC reads as non-self. Distinct from class restriction.
class restriction: The rule that CD4 reads class II and CD8 reads class I (the numbers multiply to 8).
proteasome: Cytosolic protease that generates class I peptides; IFN-gamma induces the immunoproteasome for better anchor residues.
TAP: Transporter associated with antigen processing: ATP-dependent pump moving cytosolic peptides into the ER for class I loading; its loss causes Bare Lymphocyte Syndrome type I.
tapasin: ER chaperone that docks the class I molecule at TAP for peptide loading.
calnexin: ER chaperone stabilizing the empty class I alpha chain until beta-2-microglobulin binds.
cathepsin: Acidic protease in the phagolysosome that generates class II peptides (the class II analog of the proteasome).
invariant chain: (Ii) Chaperones class II folding, BLOCKS the cleft from endogenous peptide, and ROUTES class II to the vesicular compartment; trimmed to leave CLIP.
CLIP: The invariant-chain remnant left sitting in the class II groove until HLA-DM swaps it for antigenic peptide.
HLA-DM: Accessory (non-presenting) molecule that removes CLIP and loads antigenic peptide into the class II cleft.
CD1: Class I-like molecule (with beta-2-microglobulin) that presents LIPID/glycolipid antigens to NKT/gamma-delta cells; traffics by the class II vesicular pathway.
endogenous: Antigen synthesized in the CYTOSOL, presented on MHC class I to CD8 cells.
exogenous: Antigen taken into a VESICLE (including intravesicular bugs like Mycobacterium/Listeria), presented on MHC class II to CD4 cells.
TCR: T-cell receptor: an alpha-beta heterodimer that recognizes peptide on MHC (never free antigen) and is NEVER secreted; uses CD3/zeta for signaling.
BCR: B-cell receptor: surface immunoglobulin (two heavy + two light chains) that binds NATIVE unprocessed antigen directly; signals via Igalpha/Igbeta.
CD3: Invariant signaling complex of the TCR carrying the ITAMs that LCK phosphorylates; the TCR itself does not signal.
ITAM: Immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motif: phosphorylated docking sequence on CD3/zeta (TCR) or Igalpha/Igbeta (BCR) that recruits ZAP-70/Syk.
zeta: The TCR zeta (ITAM-bearing) signaling chains, partnered with CD3.
LCK: Src-family kinase that phosphorylates the CD3/zeta ITAMs, creating docking sites for ZAP-70.
ZAP-70: Indispensable hub kinase of TCR signaling; docks on phosphorylated ITAMs and phosphorylates LAT. Its loss means NO T-cell response.
LAT: Scaffold phosphorylated by ZAP-70 that branches TCR signaling into the MAPK, NF-kB, and NFAT pathways.
Syk: The B-cell equivalent of ZAP-70; recruited to phosphorylated Igalpha/Igbeta ITAMs to transduce BCR signal 1.
Igalpha: Signaling chain (with Igbeta) carrying the BCR's ITAMs; phosphorylated by Lyn, then recruits Syk.
PKC: Protein kinase C: activates the NF-kB arm of TCR signaling (via the IKK).
calcineurin: Calcium/calmodulin-activated phosphatase that dephosphorylates NFAT; the target of cyclosporine and tacrolimus.
calmodulin: Calcium sensor that activates calcineurin in the NFAT arm of TCR signaling.
CD28: Co-stimulatory receptor on T cells (the gas/amplifier); binds B7 on the APC to deliver signal 2.
CTLA-4: Inhibitory receptor (a brake) that outcompetes CD28 for the SAME B7, arresting expansion ~day 3-4; involved in the anergy/T1D checkpoint.
PD-1: Inhibitory receptor on T cells; engagement by PD-L1 shuts off effector killing; blocked by pembrolizumab.
CD25: IL-2 receptor alpha chain; transiently upregulated by IL-2 to open an expansion window; also a Treg marker.
CCR7: Lymph-node homing chemokine receptor; central-memory T cells keep it (stay in node), effector-memory lose it. Required for HEV entry into nodes.
CXCR5: Follicle-homing chemokine receptor (follows CXCL13); naive/follicular B cells use it to enter the B-cell follicle.
CD40L: CD40 ligand on the T cell; induces AID (class switching), partners with IFN-gamma for macrophage killing, and can REVERSE B-cell anergy.
CD40: B-cell/macrophage receptor for CD40L; the help signal that induces AID; its loss causes hyper-IgM (HIGM-3).
superantigen: An antigen that bridges TCR V-beta to MHC II OUTSIDE the peptide groove, polyclonally activating up to ~20% of T cells (toxic shock).
mitogen: A substance driving polyclonal lymphocyte proliferation through stimulatory receptors (e.g. TLR), independent of antigen specificity.
hapten: A small molecule that BINDS (antigen) but is not immunogenic until coupled to a carrier protein (e.g. penicillin on RBCs causing drug-induced hemolytic anemia).
haptenation: Covalent attachment of a drug (hapten) onto a host cell (e.g. RBC), generating a neo-antigen that triggers IgG.
antigen: Anything that binds an immune receptor or antibody; it need NOT induce a response.
immunogen: An antigen that actually INDUCES an immune response; all immunogens are antigens but not vice versa.
epitope: The specific region of an antigen actually recognized by a receptor/antibody; one antigen carries multiple epitopes.
epitope spreading: Progressive broadening of an autoimmune response to neighboring self-epitopes as tissue destruction releases new antigens (drives chronicity in SLE).
alloantigen: An antigen that differs WITHIN a species (e.g. donor MHC in transplant).
autoantigen: A self-antigen targeted in autoimmunity; cannot be cleared, making autoimmune disease chronic.
affinity: Strength of drug-receptor binding, measured by KD (the equilibrium dissociation constant, i.e. the concentration occupying 50% of receptors). Higher affinity = LOWER KD (inverse). High affinity does not guarantee high efficacy.
avidity: Total combined binding strength of all sites (multivalent); IgM has modest affinity per arm but high avidity from ten sites.
Fab: The antigen-binding arm of an antibody (variable + part of constant); papain yields two separate Fabs.
Papain: Protease that cleaves antibody ABOVE the hinge into 2 separate Fab + 1 Fc.
pepsin: Protease that cleaves antibody BELOW the hinge into one F(ab')2 (still cross-links antigen) and chops the Fc into small fragments.
CDR: Complementarity-determining region: one of three hypervariable loops per variable domain; the CDRs form the antigen-contact surface.
CDR3: The most diverse, most antigen-specific CDR because it spans the V(D)J segment junction; the sole target of junctional diversity.
IgM: First isotype made and first surface BCR; pentameric with high avidity; the most efficient COMPLEMENT activator; stays mostly intravascular.
IgG: Most abundant serum isotype with the LONGEST half-life (FcRn recycling); the ONLY isotype crossing the placenta; neutralizes and opsonizes.
IgA: Dominant MUCOSAL isotype (secretory IgA); ~90% of breast-milk immunoglobulin; transported across epithelium by pIgR.
IgE: Trace serum isotype bound to mast cells/basophils via FcepsilonRI; mediates Type I hypersensitivity and anti-helminth ADCC; shortest half-life.
IgD: Isotype serving mainly as a surface BCR on naive mature B cells; co-expressed with IgM by alternative splicing.
SIgA: Secretory IgA: dimeric IgA carried across epithelium by pIgR, retaining the secretory piece; the signature mucosal antibody.
pIgR: Polymeric Ig receptor: binds the J chain of dimeric IgA, transcytoses it, and is cleaved to leave the secretory piece. Its loss means no luminal SIgA.
J chain: Polypeptide that joins polymeric IgA/IgM, provides structural stability, and is bound by pIgR for transcytosis.
secretory piece: The cleaved pIgR remnant remaining on secretory IgA, protecting it in the lumen.
FcRn: Neonatal Fc receptor: carries IgG across the placenta AND recycles serum IgG, giving IgG the longest half-life (explains the 3-6 month infant gap).
FcgammaRI: High-affinity phagocyte Fc receptor for IgG driving opsonization.
FcgammaRIII: NK-cell Fc receptor (alias CD16) that binds IgG to mediate ADCC.
FcalphaRI: Phagocyte Fc receptor (CD89) for IgA driving opsonization.
FcepsilonRI: High-affinity mast-cell/basophil receptor for IgE; cross-linking triggers degranulation (Type I hypersensitivity).
opsonization: Coating of a microbe by antibody (IgG/IgA) or C3b so phagocyte Fc/complement receptors grab and engulf it; key for encapsulated bacteria.
ADCC: Antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity: an NK cell binds IgG on a target via CD16 (FcgammaRIII) and kills via perforin/granzyme.
neutralization: Antibody (IgG/IgA) physically BLOCKING a pathogen or toxin from attaching to host-cell receptors.
AID: Activation-induced cytidine deaminase: the single enzyme behind BOTH somatic hypermutation and class switching; deaminates cytosine to uracil. Lost in hyper-IgM (HIGM-2).
UNG: Uracil-N-glycosylase: in class-switch recombination, removes the uracil AID created, letting APE1 nick the abasic site.
somatic hypermutation: AID-driven point mutation across the V region in germinal centers; antigen-DEPENDENT, B-cell only, drives affinity maturation.
class switching: Recombination of the heavy-chain CONSTANT region to change isotype while keeping the same V region (same specificity); induced by CD40L + cytokine.
germinal center: Clonal follicular reaction (B cells against ONE antigen) where somatic hypermutation and class switching occur; absent in XLA.
centroblast: The proliferating, surface-Ig-OFF, hypermutating germinal-center B cell.
centrocyte: The germinal-center B cell after it finishes mutating and re-expresses surface Ig (renamed from centroblast).
affinity maturation: Selection in the germinal center of B-cell clones whose hypermutated BCRs bind antigen with higher affinity.
plasma cell: Terminally differentiated antibody-SECRETING B cell; long-lived plasma cells reside in marrow and secrete for years.
memory B cell: A B cell that does NOT secrete antibody; carries a BCR and waits as the reservoir for a fast recall response.
follicular B cell: (B-2) Conventional B cell requiring CD4 help, class-switching, and generating memory.
marginal-zone B cell: Spleen emergency B cell making rapid T-INDEPENDENT IgM against blood-borne carbohydrate within hours.
B-1 cell: Innate-like B cell making fast T-independent IgM against carbohydrate antigens.
T-independent: Antigen (non-protein: polysaccharide/lipid/nucleic acid) that cannot load on MHC, recruits no T help, and gives low-affinity IgM with NO memory.
T-dependent: Protein antigen presented on MHC to TFH cells, yielding high-affinity, class-switched antibody plus memory.
CR2: Complement receptor 2 (CD21): binds C3d as part of the B-cell co-receptor to lower the activation threshold; also the EBV entry receptor.
CD19: Signaling/amplifier chain of the B-cell co-receptor (amplifies BCR signaling up to 10,000-fold); marker of mature B cells. Its loss gives low antibody and poor switching.
CD20: Mature B-cell surface marker; target of rituximab (anti-CD20).
CD21: Complement receptor 2 (CR2), the B-cell co-receptor component binding C3d; also the EBV entry receptor.
CD81: B-cell co-receptor component that aggregates the BCR co-receptor complex.
BTK: Bruton tyrosine kinase: the pre-B checkpoint kinase; mutation causes X-linked agammaglobulinemia (development stalls at pre-B, no antibodies, T cells spared).
XLA: X-linked agammaglobulinemia: a BTK defect blocking B-cell maturation (<1% CD19+, absent tonsils, no germinal centers); treated with lifelong IVIg.
RAG: Recombination-activating gene product (RAG1/RAG2): recognizes the RSS and nicks DNA within the heptamer during V(D)J recombination, leaving a hairpin.
Artemis: Endonuclease that opens the V(D)J hairpin, leaving uneven overhang ends.
TdT: Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase: adds 1-10 NON-templated (N) nucleotides at the junction, boosting CDR3 diversity.
RSS: Recombination signal sequence flanking gene segments: heptamer (palindromic, 7 bp) + spacer (12 or 23 bp) + nonamer (9 bp).
heptamer: The palindromic 7-bp portion of the RSS closest to the gene segment; aligns so RAG can nick within it.
nonamer: The 9-bp portion of the RSS farthest from the gene segment.
12/23 rule: A 12-bp-spacer RSS can join only a 23-bp-spacer RSS; like-with-like joining is FORBIDDEN, ensuring proper segment order.
allelic exclusion: Mechanism ensuring a lymphocyte expresses only the maternal OR paternal allele (one receptor per cell); the lone exception is the TCR alpha chain.
isotypic exclusion: Light-chain rule where kappa rearranges first and suppresses lambda; lambda proceeds only if kappa fails.
junctional diversity: Diversity generated at the V(D)J seam (P-nucleotides, exonuclease trimming, N-nucleotides); changes CDR3 only and causes >90% out-of-frame apoptosis.
combinatorial association: Pairing of any heavy chain with any light chain at the PROTEIN level; a B-cell-only diversity mechanism that T cells lack.
DN1: Earliest double-negative thymocyte stage where Notch1 binds cTEC Notch-ligand to commit to the T lineage.
Notch1: Receptor on early thymocytes whose signaling commits them to the T lineage; too little yields aberrant B cells in the thymus.
pre-T-alpha: Invariant surrogate alpha chain pairing with the rearranged beta chain at checkpoint 1; does NOT undergo V(D)J and is identical in everyone.
double-negative: Thymocyte expressing neither CD4 nor CD8 co-receptor; gamma-delta T cells stay double-negative.
double-positive: Thymocyte expressing both CD4 and CD8 after a complete alpha-beta TCR forms; subject to positive then negative selection.
positive selection: Cortical step selecting double-positive thymocytes that bind self-MHC at LOW affinity; establishes MHC restriction and fixes CD4 vs CD8 lineage.
negative selection: Medullary step deleting thymocytes that bind self-MHC + self-peptide at HIGH affinity; enforces central tolerance using AIRE.
death by neglect: Fate of a thymocyte recognizing NO self-MHC; the most common thymic fate.
AIRE: AutoImmune REgulator: lets mTECs express tissue-restricted self-antigens for negative selection; its mutation causes autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome.
cTEC: Cortical thymic epithelial cell: provides Notch ligand + IL-7 and displays MHC for positive selection.
mTEC: Medullary thymic epithelial cell: presents AIRE-driven self-peptide for negative selection.
receptor editing: Persistent RAG re-rearrangement of the LIGHT chain to escape self-reactivity; a B-cell-only tolerance mechanism (T cells are simply deleted).
anergy: Functional unresponsiveness from signal 1 without co-stimulation (or chronic self-antigen via CTLA-4/PD-1); B-cell anergy is reversible by CD40L, T-cell anergy is IRREVERSIBLE.
AICD: Activation-induced cell death: Fas/FasL-driven apoptosis of activated T cells (peripheral deletion); the extrinsic/death-receptor route.
Fas: Death receptor that, when bound by FasL, assembles the DISC to activate caspase-8 (extrinsic apoptosis).
FasL: Fas ligand; engages Fas to trigger the extrinsic death-receptor apoptosis pathway (AICD, lupus deletion arm).
DISC: Death-inducing signaling complex assembled at Fas; activates initiator caspase-8.
caspase-8: Initiator caspase of the EXTRINSIC (death-receptor) apoptosis pathway, activated at the DISC.
caspase-1: Inflammasome caspase that cleaves pro-IL-1beta into active IL-1beta (not an apoptotic effector caspase).
c-FLIP: Anti-apoptotic protein that blocks the death-receptor route by outcompeting caspase-8 at the DISC; upregulated by tumors to escape Fas killing.
BCL-2: Anti-apoptotic protein blocking mitochondrial MOMP; overexpressed by tumors to resist intrinsic apoptosis despite constant proliferation.
perforin: Cytotoxic protein that polymerizes into a membrane pore, letting granzymes enter the target's cytosol; used by CTLs and NK cells.
granzyme: Cytotoxic protease entering through the perforin pore to activate caspases and drive target apoptosis.
CTL: Cytotoxic T lymphocyte: an activated CD8 cell that kills MHC-I+antigen-bearing INFECTED host cells via perforin/granzyme and Fas (an indirect kill).
NK cell: Natural killer cell: a lymphoid innate cell (CD56+ CD16+ CD3-) that kills cells which LOSE MHC I (missing-self) and mediates ADCC.
NKG2D: Activating NK/gamma-delta receptor that binds stress ligands MIC-A/MIC-B on stressed or infected cells.
MIC-A: Stress ligand displayed by stressed epithelial cells; engaged by NKG2D on gamma-delta IELs to trigger killing.
NKT: Natural killer T cell; invariant NKT (iNKT) cells recognize lipid on CD1; non-classical NKT cells drive the atypical Th2 response in ulcerative colitis.
CD16: FcgammaRIII on NK cells, the Fc receptor mediating ADCC.
CD4: Co-receptor on helper T cells reading peptide on MHC class II; an activated CD4 cell licenses B cells (humoral immunity).
CD8: Co-receptor on cytotoxic T cells reading peptide on MHC class I; an activated CD8 cell becomes a CTL (cell-mediated immunity).
gamma-delta: T cells that exit the thymus early with NO selection, stay double-negative, guard mucosa/skin, and recognize lipid on CD1; ~10% of intestinal IELs.
IEL: Intraepithelial lymphocyte: a T cell residing within gut epithelium; ~10% are gamma-delta cells.
M cell: Microfold cell over a Peyer's patch that transcytoses luminal antigen UNALTERED to the underlying lymphoid tissue; exploited by Shigella, Salmonella, Listeria, Yersinia.
Peyer's patch: Organized GALT inductive site in the small intestine where mucosal B cells switch and undergo SHM before leaving for the mesenteric node.
Paneth cell: Small-intestinal crypt cell making alpha-defensins, lysozyme, and REG III lectins constitutively.
defensin: Antimicrobial peptide that forms PORES in microbial membranes causing osmotic lysis; alpha-defensins dominate the small intestine, beta-defensins the large.
lysozyme: Enzyme that hydrolyzes the NAM-NAG bond of peptidoglycan; GRAM-POSITIVE bacteria (thick exposed wall) are most susceptible.
lactoferrin: Iron-sequestering antimicrobial protein; bacteria counter with siderophores to steal the iron back.
siderophore: Bacterial iron-scavenging molecule used to steal iron back from host lactoferrin/transferrin.
MAdCAM-1: Endothelial addressin on mucosal vessels that the gut-homing integrin alpha4beta7 docks on for entry into the mucosa; promotes extravasation in ulcerative colitis.
alpha4beta7: Gut-homing integrin (with CCR9) upregulated on activated mucosal lymphocytes; docks on MAdCAM-1.
MALT: Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue; O-MALT (organized: NALT/BALT/GALT/RALT) is the inductive site with follicles, D-MALT (diffuse) is the effector site.
GALT: Gut-associated lymphoid tissue (Peyer's patches, appendix); the organized inductive O-MALT site of the gut.
NALT: Nasopharynx-associated lymphoid tissue (tonsils/adenoids); an O-MALT site.
BALT: Bronchus-associated lymphoid tissue; an O-MALT site.
complement: A cascade of serum proteins providing LYSIS (MAC), OPSONIZATION (C3b/CR1), and INFLAMMATION (C3a/C5a); all three pathways converge on a C3 convertase then the MAC.
classical pathway: Complement pathway triggered by antibody (or CRP binding phosphocholine) recruiting C1, cleaving C4/C2 into the C4b2a convertase.
lectin pathway: Complement pathway where MBL+MASP binds mannose to cleave C4/C2 into the C4b2a convertase (innate, antibody-independent).
alternative pathway: Complement pathway starting spontaneously by water hydrolyzing C3 (tickover), forming the C3bBb convertase; amplified by properdin.
C3 convertase: Convergence point of all three complement pathways (classical, alternative, lectin).
C3b: Opsonin and complement building block; coats microbes for CR1-mediated phagocytosis and, added to a C3 convertase, forms the C5 convertase.
C3a: Anaphylatoxin fragment recruiting phagocytes and activating mast cells; with C5a drives inflammation.
C5a: Potent anaphylatoxin and chemoattractant; with C3a recruits phagocytes whose frustrated phagocytosis damages tissue in Type III hypersensitivity.
C3d: C3 cleavage fragment that binds CR2 (CD21) on the B-cell co-receptor to lower the B-cell activation threshold.
C4b2a: The classical/lectin C3 convertase (note the larger fragment is C2a).
C3bBb: The alternative-pathway C3 convertase; stabilized by properdin.
C3bBb3b: The alternative-pathway C5 convertase (one extra C3b shifts the active site to C5).
MAC: Mycobacterium avium complex; environmental atypical mycobacteria causing disseminated infection in AIDS; treated with ethambutol + rifampin + a macrolide.
anaphylatoxin: Complement fragment (C3a, C4a, C5a) that activates mast cells to release histamine; systemic levels drive anaphylactic shock.
properdin: Factor P: stabilizes the alternative C3 convertase (C3bBb) to amplify complement.
Factor I: Complement regulator that cleaves C3b to iC3b (with cofactors MCP/factor H), rationing C3 and releasing immune complexes from RBC CR1.
DAF: Decay-accelerating factor: a GPI-anchored host regulator that dissociates Bb to decay the convertase; lost in PNH.
Factor H: Soluble complement regulator that (like MCP) recruits factor I to cleave C3b on host surfaces, protecting self cells from the alternative pathway.
iC3b: Inactivated C3b: the product of factor I cleaving C3b (with factor H/MCP); no longer forms convertase but still serves as an opsonin via CR3.
MCP: Membrane cofactor protein: recruits factor I to cleave C3b on host cells.
CD59: GPI-anchored host regulator that blocks C9 from joining C5b-8, preventing MAC formation on self cells; lost in PNH.
CR1: Complement receptor 1 on erythrocytes/phagocytes: binds C3b to clear immune complexes (ferrying them to spleen/liver) and to opsonize.
C1q: Recognition subunit of C1 (classical pathway); its deficiency impairs apoptotic-body clearance and predisposes to SLE.
C2 kinin: Vasoactive fragment released by uncontrolled C4/C2 cleavage in C1-inhibitor deficiency, causing hereditary angioedema.
MBL: Mannose-binding lectin: an acute-phase pentraxin that with MASP binds mannose to trigger the lectin pathway.
pentraxin: Acute-phase protein family (CRP, SAA, MBL) made by hepatocytes under IL-6; CRP routes to the classical pathway, MBL to the lectin pathway.
CRP: C-reactive protein: acute-phase pentraxin binding phosphocholine to recruit C1 (classical pathway) and act as an opsonin.
hypersensitivity: An immune response that DAMAGES tissue; affects ~20% of people. Types I-IV.
anaphylaxis: Systemic type I reaction whose cause of death is DISTRIBUTIVE (vascular) shock from massive vasodilation and third-spacing of fluid (plus airway/bronchospasm).
epinephrine: Mixed alpha/beta catecholamine; first-line for ANAPHYLAXIS. Dose-dependent: low dose beta predominates, high dose alpha-1. Raises systolic, lowers diastolic.
histamine: Preformed vasoactive amine in mast-cell/basophil granules; causes vasodilation and increased postcapillary-venule permeability (endothelial contraction); released by triggers such as IgE cross-linking, C3a/C5a, and physical stimuli.
leukotriene: Newly synthesized (secondary) Type I mediator ~1,000x more potent than histamine.
mast cell: Tissue cell that degranulates on IgE-FcepsilonRI cross-linking in Type I hypersensitivity; partially activated by TLR/IL-33/C3a-C5a.
eosinophil: Granulocyte recruited/activated by IL-5 that kills helminths by IgE-mediated ADCC, dumping major basic protein onto the worm.
basophil: Circulating blood counterpart of the mast cell; similar mediators, also IgE-responsive.
sensitization: The first (asymptomatic) allergen exposure that builds allergen-specific IgE on mast cells; the reaction occurs only on re-exposure.
frustrated phagocytosis: Phagocytes binding antibody/C3b-coated tissue they cannot engulf and expelling granule enzymes, ROS, and RNS into surroundings (Type II/III tissue damage).
serum sickness: SYSTEMIC Type III immune-complex reaction appearing 7-10 days after a foreign protein (now mostly mouse monoclonal antibodies).
Arthus reaction: LOCALIZED Type III vasculitis at a repeat-injection site within 4-10 hours because preformed antibody is already present.
rheumatoid factor: Autoantibody (mostly IgM) against the Fc region of IgG; positive in ~80% of RA but not RA-specific.
ACCPA: Anti-citrullinated peptide antibody: appears in ~67% of RA patients and predicts more progressive disease.
PAD: Peptidylarginine deiminase: converts arginine to CITRULLINE on self-protein, creating the RA neo-antigen.
citrulline: Neutral residue formed when PAD deiminates arginine; the citrullinated self-protein is the RA target presented well by HLA-DR4/DR1.
anti-GBM: Anti-glomerular-basement-membrane disease: IgG against the NC1 domain of alpha-3 type IV collagen, damaging KIDNEY and LUNG (shared epitope); linked to HLA-DR2.
myasthenia gravis: Antagonistic Type II disease: antibody BLOCKS the acetylcholine receptor, causing muscle weakness; linked to HLA-B8.
Graves: Agonistic Type II disease: antibody STIMULATES the TSH receptor, causing hyperthyroidism; linked to HLA-DR3.
SLE: Systemic lupus erythematosus: impaired apoptotic-body clearance (classically C1q deficiency) spills nuclear antigens; anti-DNA antibodies; HLA-DR3; breaks the deletion (Fas/FasL) arm.
AIHA: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia: IgG autoantibodies opsonize RBCs for splenic macrophages, or IgM fixes complement for MAC lysis.
T1D: Type 1 diabetes: organ-specific autoimmunity destroying islet beta cells; susceptibility HLA-DQ2/DQ8 holds self-peptide LOOSELY (weak thymic signal lets the self-reactive T cell escape deletion); killers are CD8 CTLs (perforin/granzyme, Fas). Breaks the anergy (CTLA-4) arm.
vitiligo: Organ-specific autoimmunity where CD8+ CTLs destroy melanocytes after Tregs are downregulated; treated with JAK inhibitors (ruxolitinib) and calcineurin inhibitors.
Crohn: Th1/Th17-driven IBD affecting any segment mouth-to-anus, TRANSMURAL, with rare rectal bleeding; NOD2/MUC2 variants; IL-21 makes cytotoxic B cells.
ulcerative colitis: Atypical Th2 IBD by non-classical NKT cells (IL-4/IL-13) limited to colon/rectum, CONTINUOUS, mucosa/submucosa only, with characteristic rectal bleeding.
Guillain-Barre: Anti-ganglioside molecular mimicry after C. jejuni; gamma-delta T cells prominent (mucosal trigger); treated by plasmapheresis/IVIg.
molecular mimicry: A microbial epitope resembling a self-epitope so antibodies/T cells cross-react with self (e.g. S. pyogenes M protein to cardiac myosin in rheumatic fever).
rheumatic fever: Non-suppurative immune-mediated disease ~2-3 weeks after pharyngitis (throat now culture-negative); pancarditis is a strong criterion.
ankylosing spondylitis: Spondyloarthropathy linked to HLA-B27, associated with K. pneumoniae molecular mimicry.
granuloma: A Th1/IFN-gamma-maintained quarantine of epithelioid/giant/foamy cells walling off a persistent microbe (e.g. M. tuberculosis); reactivates if IFN-gamma or CD4 falls.
epithelioid cell: Activated macrophage in a granuloma that fuses into giant cells and lays a fibrous capsule.
caseous: The necrotic cheese-like granuloma center that spills viable bacteria when the cuff breaks.
contact hypersensitivity: Type IV reaction to a hapten + skin-protein carrier; sensitization phase builds memory Th1, effector phase fires within 24-72h via CD8 Tc1 and CD4 Th1.
passive immunity: Receiving PREFORMED antibody; immediate onset but temporary with no memory (no recipient lymphocytes involved).
active immunity: Mounting YOUR OWN immune response (infection or vaccination); slow but long-lasting with memory.
herd immunity: Once a sufficient FRACTION (not everyone) of a population is immune, transmission is interrupted, protecting the non-immune; threshold rises as R0 rises.
toxoid: An inactivated toxin used as an ACTIVE vaccine so the body makes neutralizing antitoxin; only bacterial toxoid vaccines exist.
antitoxin: Preformed antibody against a toxin given as PASSIVE immunity (contrast the active toxoid).
conjugate vaccine: Links a weak polysaccharide to a carrier protein, recruiting T-cell help to make a strong IgG response that works in children under 2.
subunit vaccine: Vaccine containing only specific antigenic proteins, not whole organisms.
IVIg: Intravenous immunoglobulin (mostly IgG): replaces missing antibody (XLA, DiGeorge, hyper-IgM) OR blocks macrophage Fc receptors (reticuloendothelial blockade in ITP).
HSCT: Hematopoietic stem-cell transplant: the only true CURE for a genetic stem-cell-level immune defect, but requires ablating the recipient's immune system first.
SCID: Severe combined immunodeficiency: an umbrella term always involving T cells plus at least one other arm; live vaccines are contraindicated.
selective IgA deficiency: Most common primary immunodeficiency: defective B-cell differentiation into IgA plasma cells (normal IgA genes); low IgA with normal IgM/IgG; treat infections, not replace IgA.
DiGeorge: 22q11.2 deletion causing thymic aplasia (CD3+ T cells <1%, normal B cells), truncus arteriosus, and low PTH/hypocalcemia; treated with thymic transplant.
hyper-IgM: Class-switch failure with high IgM:IgG/IgA ratio; HIGM-1 (CD40L) is a T-cell defect/SCID, HIGM-2 (AID) and others are B-cell forms; treated with IVIg.
BLS: Bare Lymphocyte Syndrome: type I (TAP mutation, no surface MHC I, low CD8) or type II (no MHC II, low CD4, failed T-dependent antibody); MHC genes are normal.
HLH: Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis: defective perforin/granzyme killing makes CTLs/NK keep secreting IFN-gamma, hyperactivating macrophages that phagocytose blood cells (cytopenias, splenomegaly).
CGD: Chronic granulomatous disease: defective phagocyte oxidative burst (e.g. NADPH oxidase) so ingested pathogens survive, forming granulomas.
LAD-1: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency 1: CD18/LFA-1 mutation blocking neutrophil extravasation (neutrophilia, NO pus, delayed cord separation).
ITP: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura: anti-platelet IgG opsonizes platelets for splenic destruction; low platelets with giant platelets, increased megakaryocytes, normal PT/PTT.
PNH: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria: a GPI-anchor defect so DAF/CD59 cannot attach to RBCs, letting complement lyse them.
Reed-Sternberg: Diagnostic giant cell of HODGKIN lymphoma, which spreads in an orderly node-to-node pattern.
multiple myeloma: Malignant plasma cells causing punched-out lytic bone lesions and Bence-Jones light chains that cause renal failure.
ALL: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia: the most common pediatric malignancy.
CLL: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia: mature B cells that cannot undergo apoptosis, seen in older adults.
Bence-Jones: Free monoclonal light chains in multiple myeloma that deposit in the kidney and cause renal failure.
rejection: Immune destruction of a graft: hyperacute (<=24h, preformed antibody + complement, thrombosis), acute (T cells, weeks), chronic (immune complexes + T cells, fibrosis/arteriosclerosis).
allorecognition: How the recipient sees donor MHC: DIRECT (recipient TCR sees INTACT donor MHC on graft cells; strong, drives ACUTE rejection) vs INDIRECT (recipient APC presents donor-MHC peptides on self-MHC; drives CHRONIC rejection).
GVHD: Graft-versus-host disease: donor T cells recognize recipient HLA directly and attack recipient skin, gut, and liver (~4 weeks).
Coombs: Antiglobulin test using antibodies against human IgG/IgM and C3; DIRECT (DAT) detects antibody already on RBCs in vivo, INDIRECT (IAT) detects free serum antibody.
RhoGAM: Anti-D IgG given to Rh-negative mothers; anti-D is IgG (crosses placenta, causes HDN if untreated) whereas ABO antibodies are IgM and do not cross.
Landsteiner: Rule that you make antibodies against the ABO antigens you LACK; type O is the universal RBC donor, AB the universal recipient.
tolerance: Self-non-self discrimination preventing immune attack on self; central (thymus/marrow) plus peripheral (anergy, deletion, suppression). Its failure causes autoimmunity.
respiratory burst: Phagocyte generation of reactive oxygen species via NADPH oxidase (superoxide -> SOD -> H2O2 -> MPO -> HOCl) to kill ingested microbes.
NADPH oxidase: Phagocyte enzyme converting O2 into superoxide to start the respiratory burst; defective in CGD.
MPO: Myeloperoxidase: converts H2O2 into hypochlorous acid (HOCl) in the phagosome.
SOD: Superoxide dismutase: converts superoxide into hydrogen peroxide in the ROS chain.
iNOS: Inducible nitric oxide synthase: makes nitric oxide from arginine, starting reactive nitrogen species (RNS).
catalase: Enzyme letting Staphylococcus detoxify H2O2 and resist the respiratory burst (catalase-positive organisms).
phagolysosome: Fusion of phagosome and lysosome where acid hydrolases digest the microbe at low pH; M. tuberculosis blocks its formation.
vacuolar ATPase: Pump that drives H+ into the phagosome to acidify it (pH 4-5) before digestion.
NET: Norepinephrine transporter; mediates NE reuptake (the main termination of NE action). Blocked by atomoxetine/cocaine; reversed by amphetamine.
NETosis: A distinct programmed neutrophil death (not apoptosis/necrosis) that kills extracellularly at the cost of the cell's life.
neutrophil: Most abundant blood leukocyte and first cell recruited to infected tissue (~2h); kills via phagocytosis, granules, and NETs; >5% bands = left shift.
macrophage: Tissue-resident phagocyte (undertaker of the body) that clears apoptotic cells, makes all five key cytokines, and presents antigen locally.
monocyte: Blood precursor that converts into tissue macrophages (or dendritic cells) after entering tissue.
dendritic cell: THE primer of naive T cells; traffics antigen from tissue to the lymph node and, once TLR-matured, delivers all three activation signals.
Kupffer cell: Liver-resident macrophage in hepatic sinusoids that screens portal-vein blood-borne antigen.
PS-receptor: Macrophage receptor binding phosphatidylserine (the eat-me signal) on apoptotic cells; faulty clearance contributes to lupus.
phosphatidylserine: The eat-me signal flipped to the outer leaflet of apoptotic cells, recognized by the PS-receptor.
selectin: Adhesion molecule mediating leukocyte ROLLING, the first step of leukocyte trafficking.
integrin: Adhesion molecule (e.g. LFA-1) mediating FIRM ARREST of leukocytes after selectin rolling.
LFA-1: Leukocyte integrin binding endothelial ICAM-1 for firm arrest; also sustains DC-T contact. Mutated (CD18) in LAD-1.
ICAM-1: Endothelial ligand for LFA-1 in firm arrest; also the rhinovirus receptor.
diapedesis: Leukocyte migration across the endothelium into tissue after chemokine signaling.
extravasation: Leukocyte exit from blood into tissue (rolling, arrest, diapedesis); blocked in LAD-1.
HEV: High endothelial venule: specialized vessel through which naive B/T cells enter lymph nodes, requiring L-selectin, an integrin, and CCR7.
PALS: Periarteriolar lymphatic sheath: the T-cell zone of the splenic white pulp.
thoracic duct: Main lymphatic vessel draining everything except the right upper quadrant into the left subclavian vein; flow boosted by lymphatic-pump techniques.
lacteal: Intestinal lymphatic that absorbs dietary fat packaged as chylomicrons.
chylomicron: Lipoprotein packaging dietary fat for absorption by gut lacteals.
spleen: Secondary lymphoid organ filtering BLOOD; red pulp removes aged RBCs, white pulp holds follicles (B) and PALS (T) plus marginal-zone B cells.
lymph node: Secondary lymphoid organ filtering tissue-derived LYMPH; follicle (B) and paracortex (T); antigen enters via afferent lymphatics carried by DCs.
thymus: Primary lymphoid organ where T cells mature; cortex (positive selection by cTECs) and medulla (negative selection by mTECs/AIRE).
HSC: Hematopoietic stem cell: pluripotent marrow cell giving rise to common lymphoid (NK/B/T) and common myeloid (everything else) progenitors.
EBV: Epstein-Barr virus; linked to Burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, NK/T-cell lymphoma, and infectious mononucleosis.
M. tuberculosis: Intracellular pathogen surviving in macrophages by blocking phagosome acidification AND lysosome fusion; walled off in Th1/IFN-gamma granulomas.
Neisseria: Encapsulated organism causing recurrent infection when the terminal complement MAC (C5-C9) is deficient.
C. difficile: Tight-junction-disrupting toxin producer that both invades tissue and causes diarrhea from fluid efflux.
C. jejuni: Gut pathogen whose ganglioside molecular mimicry triggers Guillain-Barre syndrome.
S. pyogenes: Group A strep whose M protein cross-reacts with cardiac myosin (molecular mimicry) to cause rheumatic fever.
DIC: Disseminated intravascular coagulation; a CONSUMPTIVE coagulopathy where widespread microthrombi consume platelets/factors, then secondary fibrinolysis causes bleeding.
septic shock: Body-wide vasodilation and vascular leak from SYSTEMIC TNF-alpha (circulating infected cells or blood-borne LPS).
beta-2-microglobulin: Invariant light chain that must bind the class I alpha chain (and CD1) for surface expression.
necrosis: Cell death in living tissue marked by LOSS of plasma-membrane integrity, enzyme spillage, and surrounding inflammation. The morphologic opposite of apoptosis.
pyknosis: Nuclear SHRINKAGE into a dense basophilic mass; one of the three nuclear changes of necrosis.
karyolysis: Enzymatic FADING/dissolution of the nucleus as DNases digest chromatin; a nuclear change of necrosis.
karyorrhexis: FRAGMENTATION of the nucleus into pieces; a nuclear change of necrosis.
eosinophilia: On H&E, the increased PINK cytoplasmic staining of a necrotic cell as proteins denature (also the term for elevated eosinophils in allergy/parasites).
hypoxia: Oxygen deprivation; the single MOST COMMON final pathway of cell injury, first crippling the mitochondrion's ATP production.
mitochondrion: The FIRST organelle hit in hypoxia because it can no longer make ATP; also releases cytochrome c to trigger intrinsic apoptosis.
hydroxyl radical: The MOST damaging reactive oxygen species; the cell has essentially no defense against it.
superoxide: A reactive oxygen species generated by NADPH oxidase; converted to H2O2 by superoxide dismutase.
Superoxide dismutase (SOD): Antioxidant enzyme that converts SUPEROXIDE to hydrogen peroxide (H2O2).
glutathione: Antioxidant pathway that reduces H2O2 to water, defending the cell against reactive oxygen species.
plasma-membrane integrity: The single feature whose LOSS separates irreversible necrosis from reversible injury.
hydropic change: Reversible cell swelling from water influx (ER dilation, ribosome detachment) that is fully recoverable.
lipofuscin: Brown 'wear-and-tear' pigment; an indigestible residue of LIPID PEROXIDATION that builds up in long-lived post-mitotic cells (neurons, cardiac myocytes, hepatocytes).
autophagy: A cell-survival route in which the cell digests its own organelles in lysosomes and recycles the parts, leaving lipofuscin behind.
atrophy: Reduced organ size from a decrease in cell SIZE and NUMBER, driven by ubiquitin-proteasome degradation plus autophagy.
ubiquitin-proteasome: Pathway that tags proteins with ubiquitin for proteasomal degradation; the molecular engine of atrophy.
troponin: Cardiac biomarker released into blood when an infarcted myocyte's membrane ruptures; signals MI.
CK-MB: Creatine kinase MB isoenzyme; cardiac injury marker released from dead myocytes after MI.
coagulative necrosis: Necrosis that PRESERVES tissue architecture as ghost cells (outlines intact, nuclei gone); the default for ischemic infarcts of solid organs except the brain.
liquefactive necrosis: Necrosis that DISSOLVES tissue into a soft cystic cavity; pattern of brain infarcts and bacterial abscesses.
caseous necrosis: Cheese-like friable debris of TUBERCULOSIS, enclosed within a granuloma.
fat necrosis: Chalky-white saponification of acute pancreatitis; leaked lipases free fatty acids that bind calcium.
fibrinoid necrosis: Vessel-wall pattern where immune complexes drive fibrin into the wall, leaving a bright-pink amorphous deposit.
gangrenous necrosis: Clinical label for an ischemic limb (coagulative necrosis); becomes 'wet' with superimposed bacterial infection.
PCR: Polymerase chain reaction; AMPLIFIES a nucleic acid target through cycles of denaturation, annealing, and extension, detecting even a single copy.
denaturation: PCR step where heat separates the double-stranded DNA template.
annealing: PCR step where primers bind to their complementary target sequences.
extension: PCR step where polymerase synthesizes new DNA strands.
Taq: Heat-stable DNA polymerase used in PCR because it survives the high heat of the denaturation step each cycle.
RT-PCR: Reverse-transcription PCR; detects RNA by first making cDNA (used for HIV viral load).
qPCR: Quantitative PCR; measures the AMOUNT of target (e.g., viral load); its cycle-threshold value is inversely related to load.
Southern: Hybridization blot that detects DNA (mnemonic SNOW DROP).
Western blot: Protein-detection blot; used to CONFIRM a positive HIV ELISA screen.
NGS: Next-generation sequencing; massively parallel sequencing that AMPLIFIES and reads many targets at once, trading some accuracy for huge throughput.
FISH: Fluorescence in situ hybridization; reads chromosomal LOCATION and copy number (aneuploidy, rearrangements) using fluorescent probes; confirms HER2 and BCR-ABL.
microarray: Hybridization assay comparing expression of thousands of genes at once via two-color logic (red=higher in test, green=higher in reference, yellow=equal).
Sanger: First-generation sequencing reading ~300-1000 bp; the GOLD STANDARD for single-gene testing due to high accuracy.
whole-exome: Sequencing of the ~1.5-2% of the genome that codes protein but contains >85% of known disease-causing mutations.
whole-genome: Sequencing of the entire genome; used when the target is unknown and must be discovered.
targeted multigene panel: NGS test that sequences a defined set of candidate genes at once; used when a disease could arise from many genes.
CFTR: Gene mutated in cystic fibrosis; inherited autosomal recessive.
cystic fibrosis: Autosomal recessive CFTR disease; suspect in a child with COPD-like lungs, pancreatic insufficiency, and chronic Pseudomonas colonization.
NIPT: Noninvasive prenatal test; SCREENS cell-free fetal DNA in maternal serum (~10 weeks) for trisomies 21/18/13; a positive must be confirmed by amniocentesis or CVS.
cell-free fetal DNA: Fetal DNA circulating in maternal serum, analyzed by NIPT to screen for trisomies.
amniocentesis: Invasive prenatal test that confirms a positive NIPT screen.
chorionic villus sampling (CVS): Invasive prenatal test that confirms a positive NIPT screen.
PKU: Phenylketonuria; defective phenylalanine hydroxylase causes phenylalanine buildup and cognitive impairment; treated with a phenylalanine-restricted diet.
phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH): Enzyme deficient in PKU, causing phenylalanine accumulation.
Guthrie test: Old single-analyte bacterial-inhibition newborn screen, replaced by tandem mass spectrometry.
tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS): Newborn-screening method that quantifies many metabolites from one blood spot.
liquid biopsy: Blood/urine/saliva test for circulating tumor DNA, exosomes, or circulating tumor cells; used for early detection, monitoring, and tracking residual disease.
circulating tumor DNA: Tumor-derived DNA in blood, the target of a liquid biopsy.
EGFR: Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor, a receptor tyrosine kinase whose overstimulation/mutation drives uncontrolled proliferation and cancer.
HER2: Receptor tyrosine kinase amplified in some breast cancers (confirmed by FISH); targeted by trastuzumab.
trastuzumab: Monoclonal antibody targeting HER2-amplified breast cancer.
tyrosine-kinase inhibitor (TKI): Drug class that blocks tyrosine kinase signaling (e.g., for EGFR-mutant lung cancer, BCR-ABL).
mecA: Resistance gene detected in MRSA by molecular panels.
MRSA: Methicillin-RESISTANT Staph aureus; altered PBP2a evades beta-lactams; covered by vancomycin (and 5th-gen ceftaroline, linezolid, daptomycin).
organogenesis: Weeks 3-8 of development when major structural anomalies originate.
gastrulation: Week-3 event forming the three germ layers.
neurulation: Week-3 event forming the neural tube.
neural crest: Migratory cells whose failed migration can co-produce cleft lip/palate, conotruncal heart defects, and face/arch anomalies.
malformation: INTRINSIC error in the developmental program (e.g., spina bifida, renal agenesis); morphogenesis was wrong from the start.
disruption: EXTERNAL destruction of normally developing tissue; classic example is amniotic bands.
deformation: MECHANICAL compression of normal tissue occurring LATE (~weeks 35-38); e.g., clubfoot from oligohydramnios.
dysplasia: In development, abnormal cellular organization within an organ; in neoplasia, disordered growth of abnormal-looking cells (the reversible step before cancer).
teratogen: An agent causing developmental anomalies; severity depends on timing, dose, duration, and genetic susceptibility, worst in weeks 3-8.
TORCH: Cluster of congenital infections (Toxoplasma, Other, Rubella, CMV, HSV) causing ~2-3% of anomalies.
Rubella: The FIRST recognized teratogen (1941); weeks 4-7 infection gives the triad of cataracts + deafness + heart defects.
thalidomide: Teratogen causing limb reduction/phocomelia within a narrow window of days 21-26.
valproate: Anticonvulsant teratogen causing neural tube defects by acting as a folate antagonist.
isotretinoin: Vitamin A analog (Accutane) causing craniofacial/arch, cardiac, and CNS defects; highly teratogenic even at low dose.
fetal alcohol syndrome: Teratogenic syndrome from prenatal alcohol; there is NO SAFE amount at any stage.
IUGR: Intrauterine growth restriction; e.g., from tobacco-induced placental vasoconstriction and fetal hypoxia.
neural tube defects: Anencephaly, encephalocele, and spina bifida from failed neural-tube closure; risk lowered by folic acid.
folic acid: Supplement that lowers the risk of neural tube defects.
Potter sequence: Cascade initiated by oligohydramnios (classically renal agenesis) causing limb defects, Potter facies, and lethal pulmonary hypoplasia.
oligohydramnios: Deficient amniotic fluid; the initiating error of Potter sequence.
pulmonary hypoplasia: Underdeveloped lungs; the lethal end-result of Potter sequence.
Pierre Robin sequence: Cascade initiated by micrognathia, displacing the tongue backward to cause cleft palate.
sequence: One initiating developmental error cascading into multiple anomalies.
syndrome: Diverse anomalies with a known cause but unknown mechanism (e.g., FAS).
association: Non-random co-occurrence of anomalies with UNKNOWN cause (e.g., VACTERL).
neoplasm: A group of cells of common origin that have ESCAPED normal restraints on proliferation, giving relatively autonomous growth.
parenchyma: The neoplastic cell compartment of a tumor.
stroma: The non-neoplastic supporting compartment of a tumor (vessels, immune cells, ECM).
anaplasia: IRREVERSIBLE loss of cell differentiation; features include pleomorphism, hyperchromatic nuclei, atypical mitoses, and loss of polarity.
pleomorphism: Variation in cell/nuclear size and shape; a cytologic feature of anaplasia.
basement membrane: The barrier a tumor must BRIDGE to be invasive; benign tumors and carcinoma in situ cannot cross it.
carcinoma in situ: Full malignant cytology but the basement membrane is INTACT (premalignant); cannot metastasize.
metastasis: Tumor spread to distant sites; responsible for ~90% of cancer deaths and the defining feature of malignancy.
lymphatic spread: Metastatic route typical of CARCINOMAS, reaching the sentinel node first.
sentinel: The first lymph node draining a tumor, sampled first to assess spread.
hematogenous spread: Bloodstream metastatic route typical of SARCOMAS.
transcoelomic spread: Seeding across body cavities; classic example is ovarian carcinoma seeding the peritoneum.
hyperplasia: Increased NUMBER of normal-looking cells in organized tissue; only occurs in tissues that can divide; reversible.
metaplasia: Reversible replacement of one differentiated cell type by another via stem-cell reprogramming (e.g., gastric to intestinal epithelium with goblet cells).
sarcoma: Malignant mesenchymal tumor; tends to spread hematogenously.
melanoma: An '-oma' name that is actually MALIGNANT (melanocytic cancer); stains S-100.
seminoma: An '-oma' name that is actually a MALIGNANT germ-cell tumor of the testis.
mesothelioma: An '-oma' name that is actually a MALIGNANT tumor of serosal lining (asbestos-associated).
lymphoma: An '-oma' name that is actually a MALIGNANT tumor of lymphocytes; stains CD45.
leukemia: An '-oma'-adjacent name that is actually a MALIGNANT neoplasm of bone-marrow blood-cell precursors.
teratoma: Germ-cell tumor containing tissue from more than one GERM LAYER (e.g., ovarian teratoma with hair and teeth).
grade: HISTOLOGIC estimate of malignancy based on degree of differentiation and number of mitoses.
stage: CLINICAL estimate of extent of tumor spread, scored by the TNM system.
TNM: AJCC staging system: T = tumor size/invasion, N = regional nodes, M = distant metastasis.
initiation: First step of chemical carcinogenesis: an IRREVERSIBLE DNA lesion.
promotion: Second step of carcinogenesis: REVERSIBLE clonal expansion of the mutated cell.
direct-acting carcinogen: Carcinogen needing NO metabolic activation (e.g., alkylating cyclophosphamide).
CYP-450: Cytochrome P450 enzymes that activate indirect-acting carcinogens into reactive DNA-damaging forms.
Benzo[a]pyrene: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon from grilled/charred meat; an INDIRECT carcinogen converted by CYP-450 into a reactive epoxide.
aflatoxin: Aspergillus toxin on stored grains/nuts; causes hepatocellular carcinoma.
hepatocellular carcinoma: Liver cancer linked to aflatoxin B1 and to chronic HBV/HCV-driven inflammation.
nitrosamines: Carcinogens from cured/smoked meats; cause gastric adenocarcinoma.
pyrimidine dimers: DNA lesions caused by UV light, normally removed by nucleotide-excision repair.
ionizing radiation: Radiation causing double-strand DNA breaks and chromosomal aberrations (thyroid, lung, hematologic cancers).
HPV: Human papillomavirus; high-risk types 16/18 cause cervical/oropharyngeal SCC via E6/E7 inactivating p53/Rb; low-risk 6/11 cause warts.
Burkitt lymphoma: Aggressive B-cell lymphoma with t(8;14) activating c-MYC; endemic form is EBV+ with a jaw/maxillary mass in African children.
HBV/HCV: Hepatitis B and C viruses; drive hepatocellular carcinoma via chronic inflammation and regenerative proliferation.
HTLV-1: Human T-lymphotropic virus 1; an oncogenic retrovirus.
HHV-8: Human herpesvirus 8; causative agent of Kaposi sarcoma.
H. pylori: Helicobacter pylori; the oncogenic bacterium driving gastric adenocarcinoma and lymphoma.
driver: Mutation that hits one of the four essential gene classes and CAUSES cancer (vs neutral passenger mutations).
passenger: A neutral bystander mutation scattered in the genome that does not drive cancer.
oncogene: Mutated gain-of-function version of a proto-oncogene; a SINGLE mutant allele transforms the cell (dominant).
proto-oncogene: Normal gene regulating cell growth; its hyperactive mutant form is an oncogene.
tumor suppressor: Gene whose LOSS-of-function (both alleles, recessive) permits cancer (e.g., RB, p53, APC, BRCA).
translocation: Oncogene-activating mechanism moving a gene next to a strong promoter (e.g., t(8;14), t(9;22)).
amplification: Oncogene-activating mechanism increasing gene copy number (e.g., N-MYC in neuroblastoma).
c-MYC: Proto-oncogene activated by t(8;14) in Burkitt lymphoma, driving runaway proliferation.
Philadelphia chromosome: The t(9;22) of CML, fusing BCR and ABL into a constitutive tyrosine kinase.
BCR-ABL: Constitutively active fusion tyrosine kinase from the Philadelphia chromosome in CML.
N-MYC: Oncogene activated by AMPLIFICATION in neuroblastoma (double minutes, homogeneous-staining regions).
RAS: GTPase proto-oncogene; a point mutation abolishing its GTPase activity locks it ON in the active GTP-bound state, driving proliferation.
GTPase: Enzyme activity that switches RAS off; its loss locks RAS in the active state.
E2F: Transcription factor that activates S-phase genes; held in check by active Rb.
retinoblastoma: Childhood eye tumor; familial form (germline first hit) is early/bilateral, sporadic form (two somatic hits) is late/unilateral.
p53: The 'guardian of the genome'; answers DNA damage with arrest, repair, or apoptosis; mutated in >50% of cancers.
Li-Fraumeni: Syndrome from an inherited germline p53 mutation causing markedly increased risk across many cancer types.
BRCA1/2: Tumor suppressors that repair double-strand DNA breaks by homologous recombination; germline loss raises breast and ovarian cancer risk.
BRCA2: Tumor suppressor; its germline loss drives hereditary breast/ovarian and aggressive early-onset prostate cancer.
FAP: Familial adenomatous polyposis; inherited APC tumor-suppressor loss.
BCL2: Anti-apoptotic protein; its overexpression in DLBCL makes B cells resist apoptosis (tumor grows by reduced death, not fast proliferation).
DLBCL: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma; an aggressive B-cell lymphoma, often BCL2-overexpressing.
mutator phenotype: Accelerated mutation rate from loss of DNA-repair genes; prototype is Lynch syndrome.
Lynch syndrome (HNPCC): Hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer; a mismatch-repair defect producing a mutator phenotype.
HNPCC: Hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer (Lynch syndrome); caused by mismatch-repair gene loss.
APC loss: Initiating step of the colon adenoma-carcinoma sequence.
KRAS activation: Intermediate step of the colon adenoma-carcinoma sequence.
p53 loss: Late step of the colon adenoma-carcinoma sequence yielding carcinoma.
DNA methylation: Epigenetic mechanism silencing genes without changing the DNA sequence; altered in cancer.
telomerase: Enzyme that rebuilds telomeres; normally active in germ/stem cells, silenced in somatic cells, and reactivated in 85-95% of cancers to achieve replicative immortality.
telomeres: Chromosome-end caps that shorten each division (the end-replication problem); rebuilt by telomerase.
matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs): Enzymes cancer cells use to degrade basement membrane and invade.
Warburg: Effect in which cancer cells perform aerobic glycolysis (glucose to lactate WITH oxygen), freeing carbon intermediates for biosynthesis; lights tumors up on FDG-PET.
aerobic glycolysis: Glycolysis to lactate despite available oxygen; the metabolic basis of the Warburg effect.
GLUT1: Glucose transporter upregulated by oncogenes/HIF-1alpha in the Warburg effect, driving high glucose uptake.
FDG-PET: Imaging that detects high tumor glucose uptake (Warburg effect) using radiolabeled glucose analog.
replicative immortality: Cancer hallmark of unlimited division via telomerase-rebuilt telomeres.
angiogenesis: Cancer hallmark of new blood-vessel formation, mainly by VEGF-driven sprouting.
immune surveillance: Constant immune scanning to find and destroy emerging cancer cells; evidenced by increased cancer in immunodeficient patients.
dendritic cells: Antigen-presenting cells that phagocytose tumor cells and present antigen on MHC class I to prime naive CD8+ T cells.
CD8+ cytotoxic: T cells primed by MHC-I-presented tumor antigen that migrate to and kill the tumor.
immune checkpoints: Inhibitory signals that keep T-cell activation within limits and protect against autoimmunity; exploited by tumors.
ipilimumab: Anti-CTLA-4 antibody that restores CD28-B7 costimulation so the CD8+ T cell activates and kills the tumor.
PD-L1: Ligand upregulated on tumor cells that binds PD-1 to deliver a direct inhibitory (off) signal at the effector stage; blocked by atezolizumab.
PD-1/PD-L1: Checkpoint axis that blocks EFFECTOR T-cell killing at the tumor (contrast: CTLA-4 blocks priming).
pembrolizumab: Anti-PD-1 checkpoint inhibitor mAb, freeing T cells to attack melanoma and other cancers.
atezolizumab: Anti-PD-L1 antibody that restores tumor killing.
CAR: Chimeric antigen receptor; fuses an antibody-derived antigen-recognition domain to intracellular T-cell signaling domains.
CAR-T: Chimeric Antigen Receptor T-cell therapy; engineers the patient's own T cells against a tumor antigen (e.g. CD19); for hematologic cancers; signature cytokine-release syndrome.
leukapheresis: Procedure harvesting a patient's T cells for CAR-T manufacturing.
cytokine release syndrome: Signature serious complication of CAR-T therapy from massive cytokine release.
biopsy with microscopic examination: The GOLD STANDARD for cancer diagnosis.
core needle: Biopsy that preserves tissue ARCHITECTURE, more informative than FNA's cell suspension.
fine-needle aspiration (FNA): Biopsy yielding only a cell suspension (no architecture).
frozen section: Fast lower-quality cryosection used mainly for intraoperative diagnosis, Mohs margins, and sentinel node assessment.
Mohs surgery: Layer-by-layer excision clearing skin-cancer margins, using frozen sections.
sentinel lymph node biopsy: Sampling the first draining node to assess metastatic spread, often by frozen section.
IHC: Immunohistochemistry; detects PROTEIN antigens in tissue, visualized as a brown DAB precipitate.
DAB: The brown chromogenic precipitate marking where an antigen is detected in immunohistochemistry.
S-100: IHC marker of MELANOMA (and neural crest tumors).
CD45: IHC marker of LYMPHOMA (leukocyte common antigen).
flow cytometry: Technique classifying leukemias/lymphomas by cell-surface clusters of differentiation using fluorophore-tagged antibodies.
clusters of differentiation (CDs): Cell-surface markers used by flow cytometry to classify blood-cell malignancies.
Type I hypersensitivity: IgE-mediated immediate reaction with mast cells/basophils; requires PRIOR sensitization; early vasodilation then late eosinophil-rich phase.
anaphylactoid: Non-IgE reaction causing DIRECT mast-cell degranulation with NO prior sensitization (radiocontrast, opiates, vancomycin).
atopic: Genetic hyper-responder phenotype making high IgE with abundant IL-4-producing TH2 cells.
Type II hypersensitivity: IgG or IgM directed against antigens on the CELL SURFACE (e.g., Graves, myasthenia, Rh disease).
natural killer (NK): Lymphocyte that lyses antibody-coated target cells in ADCC via Fc binding.
Rh disease: Hemolytic disease of the newborn; maternal IgG (not IgM) crosses the placenta to lyse fetal red cells; prevented by RhoGAM.
hydrops fetalis: Severe fetal edema from hemolysis (e.g., in Rh disease).
RhoGAM (anti-D): Anti-D immunoglobulin given at 12 and 28 weeks to tie up Rh antigen and prevent Rh sensitization.
Graves disease: Type II STIMULATORY antibody against the TSH receptor with no feedback off-switch, causing relentless hyperthyroidism.
TSH receptor: Target of the stimulatory antibody in Graves disease.
acetylcholine receptor: Target blocked by the inhibitory antibody in myasthenia gravis.
Type III hypersensitivity: Soluble immune complexes lodge in vessel walls, fix complement, and recruit neutrophils; classic triad is glomerulonephritis, arthritis, and vasculitis.
soluble immune complexes: Antigen-antibody complexes that deposit in vessels to drive type III hypersensitivity.
Type IV hypersensitivity: DELAYED, antibody-free reaction driven by TH1/TH17 T cells (e.g., PPD, contact dermatitis, granulomas).
PPD: Tuberculin skin test; a type IV reaction peaking at 48-72 hours with a perivascular mononuclear infiltrate.
Langhans: Giant cell with nuclei arranged around the PERIPHERY (vs random in foreign-body giant cells).
interferon-gamma: TH1 cytokine that activates macrophages and matures them into giant/epithelioid cells in granulomas.
TNF: Cytokine that pulls monocytes into granulomas and maintains them; very high levels cause septic shock; anti-TNF biologics risk TB reactivation.
ANA: Antinuclear antibody; the sensitive but non-specific SCREENING test for SLE.
dsDNA: Anti-double-stranded-DNA antibody; SPECIFIC for SLE and tied to the homogeneous ANA pattern.
homogeneous: ANA staining pattern (anti-dsDNA/histone) that is most common in lupus.
speckled: ANA staining pattern (anti-RNP and other extractable nuclear antigens); per this course, points toward scleroderma/mixed connective tissue disease.
lupus anticoagulant: Antiphospholipid antibody that PROLONGS the PTT in vitro but FAVORS clotting (thrombosis, miscarriage) in vivo.
antiphospholipid syndrome: Hypercoagulable state from antiphospholipid antibodies causing thrombosis and recurrent miscarriage.
drug-induced lupus: Skin-only lupus from procainamide, hydralazine, or isoniazid that resolves once the drug is stopped (spares organs).
Libman-Sacks: Sterile verrucous (nonbacterial) valve vegetations of SLE on the mitral/aortic valves.
self-tolerance: The state whose LOSS underlies every autoimmune disease.
rheumatic heart disease: Post-streptococcal disease where anti-M-protein antibodies cross-react with cardiac antigens, causing valvulitis and Aschoff bodies.
M-proteins: Streptococcal surface proteins whose antibodies cross-react with cardiac antigens in rheumatic fever.
Aschoff bodies: Myocardial foci of inflammatory destruction characteristic of rheumatic heart disease.
lupus nephritis: SLE kidney injury classified as diffuse proliferative, focal proliferative, or membranous (class V).
hydroxychloroquine: First-line SLE treatment, before glucocorticoids and cytotoxics.
VDRL: Syphilis screening test that can be falsely positive in SLE because anti-cardiolipin cross-reacts with the cardiolipin antigen.
cardiolipin: Phospholipid antigen used in the VDRL test, cross-reacted by lupus antiphospholipid antibodies.
Sjogren: Autoimmune destruction of lacrimal and salivary glands causing dry eyes and dry mouth; anti-SS-A/SS-B; raises B-cell lymphoma risk.
keratoconjunctivitis sicca: Dry eyes; a sicca feature of Sjogren syndrome.
xerostomia: Dry mouth; a sicca feature of Sjogren syndrome.
lip biopsy: Minor-salivary-gland biopsy confirming Sjogren by showing a lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate.
scleroderma: Autoimmune fibrosing disease; diffuse form is widespread with early visceral involvement (anti-Scl-70), limited form is confined with late involvement (anti-centromere, CREST).
CREST: Limited-scleroderma syndrome: Calcinosis, Raynaud, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia.
Raynaud: Episodic digital vasospasm; the 'R' of CREST.
Sclerodactyly: Tight thickened skin of the fingers; the 'S' of CREST.
Telangiectasia: Dilated small vessels; the 'T' of CREST.
pulmonary arterial hypertension: Leading cause of death in scleroderma, from an obliterative vasculopathy.
IgG4-related disease: Fibroinflammatory disease showing storiform (cartwheel) fibrosis, obliterative phlebitis, and elevated serum IgG4.
storiform (cartwheel): The cartwheel fibrosis pattern characteristic of IgG4-related disease.
Bruton: X-linked agammaglobulinemia; mutated Btk arrests B cells at the pre-B stage (T cells intact); declares after ~6 months as maternal IgG wanes.
Btk (Bruton tyrosine kinase): Kinase mutated in Bruton agammaglobulinemia, blocking B-cell maturation.
encapsulated: Encapsulated bacteria (e.g., S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, N. meningitidis) that recurrently infect Bruton/asplenic patients, who cannot opsonize them well.
ADA: Adenosine deaminase; its deficiency causes autosomal-recessive SCID by letting toxic deoxyadenosine kill dividing lymphocytes.
gamma-chain / IL-7 receptor: Defect causing X-linked SCID (common gamma chain).
Wiskott-Aldrich: X-linked WASP-defect triad of thrombocytopenia + eczema + recurrent infections, with low IgM and normal IgG.
splenectomy: Cause of secondary immunodeficiency via decreased phagocytosis/clearance of (especially encapsulated) microbes.
HIV: Human immunodeficiency virus; high polymerase error rate drives rapid resistance; treated with combinations of RT inhibitors, protease inhibitors, integrase/entry/fusion inhibitors.
ACE2: Cellular receptor for SARS-CoV-2 spike protein, explaining its lung/heart/kidney/gut tropism.
gp120: HIV envelope protein that binds CD4 first.
gp41: HIV envelope protein that mediates membrane fusion after coreceptor engagement.
CCR5: Chemokine coreceptor used by M-tropic (R5) HIV; the dominant early strain.
CXCR4: Chemokine coreceptor used by T-tropic (X4) HIV.
ELISA: Sensitive HIV SCREENING assay (~99% sensitive), confirmed by Western blot.
viral load (RT-PCR): RT-PCR measurement of HIV RNA giving the set-point that predicts CD4+ decline and tracks progression.
set-point: The viral load level after acute HIV that predicts the rate of CD4+ decline and disease progression.
Kaposi sarcoma: AIDS-defining malignancy of ENDOTHELIAL cells caused by HHV-8.
B-cell lymphoma: An AIDS-defining malignancy; also a long-term complication of Sjogren syndrome.
amyloid: Misfolded protein in a BETA-PLEATED SHEET conformation; stains Congo red with apple-green birefringence under polarized light.
Congo red: Stain that identifies amyloid, producing apple-green birefringence under polarized light.
apple-green birefringence: The polarized-light signature of Congo-red-stained amyloid.
beta-pleated sheet: The structural hallmark conformation of misfolded amyloid protein.
A-beta: Amyloid derived from amyloid precursor protein (APP) forming Alzheimer plaques.
amyloid precursor protein (APP): The precursor of A-beta amyloid in Alzheimer disease.
SA/AV nodes: Conduction nodes near which cardiac amyloid deposits to cause arrhythmia.
Warthin-Finkeldey: Giant cells of MEASLES; a viral cytopathic effect with random fused nuclei (NOT a granuloma).
Cowdry type A: Intranuclear eosinophilic inclusion with a clear halo and chromatin margination; seen in HSV/VZV.
owl's-eye: Intranuclear basophilic inclusion in a markedly enlarged cell; the cytopathic hallmark of CMV.
CMV: Cytomegalovirus; reactivates when cell-mediated immunity falls, causing owl's-eye pneumonitis, colitis, and retinitis.
Negri bodies: Intracytoplasmic eosinophilic neuronal inclusions of RABIES (hippocampus, Purkinje cells).
rabies: Virus producing cytoplasmic Negri bodies in neurons (the cytoplasmic location distinguishes it from herpesviruses).
JC virus: Polyomavirus causing PML with ground-glass intranuclear inclusions in oligodendrocytes and demyelination.
latent: Viral pattern: dormant with no continuous virions but reactivates (e.g., herpes).
productive: Viral pattern: continuously replicating, driving immune-mediated organ injury (e.g., HBV).
HSV: Herpes simplex virus; HSV-1 encephalitis causes hemorrhagic necrosis of the temporal lobe; produces Cowdry type A inclusions.
VZV: Varicella-zoster virus; causes chickenpox then dermatomal shingles on reactivation.
EBER: EBV-encoded RNA in situ stain confirming EBV in nasopharyngeal carcinoma and NK/T-cell lymphoma.
nasopharyngeal carcinoma: Non-keratinizing EBV+ (EBER-confirmed) carcinoma classic in China/Malaysia/Singapore.
carbuncle: Cluster of connected furuncles (multiple follicles, deeper) on the Staph skin-depth ladder.
phlegmon: Diffuse spreading soft-tissue infection on the Staph skin-depth ladder.
abscess: Localized collection of pus walled off by fibrous tissue, relatively inaccessible to the circulation.
Toxic shock syndrome (TSS): TSST-1 superantigen-driven cytokine storm causing fever, erythroderma, and SHOCK.
TSST-1: Staphylococcal superantigen driving toxic shock syndrome.
SSSS: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome; exfoliative toxin cleaves desmoglein-1 to peel skin, with NO shock.
exfoliative toxin: Staph toxin that cleaves desmoglein-1 to cause scalded skin syndrome.
desmoglein-1: Epidermal adhesion protein cleaved by exfoliative toxin in SSSS.
lobar pneumonia: Pneumonia progressing congestion to red hepatization to gray hepatization to resolution; #1 cause is pneumococcus.
red hepatization: Lobar-pneumonia stage with RBC-filled, liver-like consolidated lung.
gray hepatization: Lobar-pneumonia stage of fibrinopurulent, gray consolidated lung after red hepatization.
Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus): #1 cause of lobar pneumonia; lancet-shaped gram-positive diplococci on Gram stain.
Waterhouse-Friderichsen: Fulminant meningococcemia syndrome: petechiae + DIC + septic shock + bilateral adrenal hemorrhage.
diphtheria: Corynebacterium diphtheriae infection with a gray adherent pseudomembrane that bleeds when scraped, plus exotoxin myocarditis.
pseudomembrane: Gray adherent oropharyngeal membrane of diphtheria that bleeds when scraped.
pertussis: Bordetella pertussis (gram-NEGATIVE); paroxysmal cough with an inspiratory whoop.
epiglottitis: Haemophilus influenzae type b disease in young children (also meningitis).
Legionnaires' disease: Severe Legionella pneumonia (vs the self-limited flu-like Pontiac fever).
Pontiac fever: Self-limited flu-like Legionella illness with NO pneumonia.
Legionella: Bacterium that multiplies inside alveolar macrophages; cleared by a Th1/IFN-gamma response.
Pseudomonas: Opportunist causing ecthyma gangrenosum (neutropenic), malignant otitis externa (diabetic), and chronic colonization (cystic fibrosis).
necrotizing (malignant) otitis externa: Severe Pseudomonas ear infection in a long-standing diabetic with canal granulation tissue.
ecthyma gangrenosum: Black necrotic skin lesion with a red rim from Pseudomonas sepsis in a neutropenic patient.
healthspan: The years of life spent in GOOD HEALTH (vs longevity = total years lived).
longevity: The total number of years lived.
maximal life span: The theoretical ceiling on how long a species can live (~115 years in humans).
Hayflick limit: The ~50-doubling point at which telomere shortening forces replicative senescence.
replicative senescence: Irreversible cell-division arrest once telomeres reach a critical length; acts as a tumor-suppressing mechanism.
caloric restriction: Life-extending intervention that up-regulates sirtuins and lowers insulin/IGF-1 and TOR signaling.
sirtuins: NAD-dependent deacetylases (e.g., SIRT1) linking low-calorie nutrient sensing to longevity.
TOR: Nutrient-sensing protein kinase regulating growth and metabolism; lowered by caloric restriction.
stem-cell exhaustion: Aging mechanism of declining stem-cell numbers and regenerative capacity, so tissues repair slowly and less completely.
progeria: Hutchinson-Gilford progeria; LMNA mutation makes defective lamin A (progerin), with infantile onset and death in the teens from heart disease.
LMNA: Gene mutated in Hutchinson-Gilford progeria, producing defective lamin A.
progerin: The defective lamin A protein produced in Hutchinson-Gilford progeria.
Werner syndrome: 'Adult progeria' from WRN (DNA helicase) loss; cataracts + atherosclerosis + osteoporosis, dying in the 50s.
WRN: Gene encoding a DNA helicase; its loss causes Werner syndrome (adult progeria).
Cockayne syndrome: ERCC8/ERCC6 defect impairing transcription-coupled DNA repair; COFS form with photosensitivity and ~12-year life expectancy.
inflammation: Local AND systemic reaction of tissues and the microcirculation to a pathogenic insult; acute (neutrophil-driven) or chronic (lymphocyte/macrophage-driven).
vasodilation: Arteriolar widening that increases blood flow, producing rubor (redness) and calor (warmth).
bradykinin: Kinin-system mediator causing increased permeability, vasodilation, and pain.
postcapillary venules: The vessel segment whose increased permeability is the hallmark of acute inflammation.
exudate: Protein-rich inflammatory fluid filling alveoli in pneumonia; with decreased surfactant it causes congestion and impaired gas exchange.
transudate: Protein-POOR fluid with few cells from a hydrostatic/oncotic pressure problem (heart failure, nephrotic syndrome); NOT inflammation.
pyrogens: Fever-inducing agents (e.g., LPS) that drive macrophages to release IL-1, IL-6, and TNF, resetting the hypothalamic set point.
neutrophilia: Elevated blood neutrophils signaling acute bacterial infection OR sterile necrosis (including MI).
eosinophils: Bilobed red-granule cells predominating in allergic reactions and parasitic infestations.
rolling: The earliest leukocyte-recruitment step (loose tethering), mediated by selectins.
firm adhesion: Leukocyte-recruitment step after rolling, mediated by integrins.
chemotaxis: Directed leukocyte migration toward chemoattractants (C5a, formylated peptides, LTB4, chemokines).
selectins: Endothelial molecules mediating the rolling step of leukocyte recruitment.
integrins: Molecules mediating firm leukocyte adhesion to endothelium.
LTB4: Leukotriene that is a potent NEUTROPHIL chemoattractant.
lymphadenitis: Inflammation of draining lymph nodes (enlarging by follicular hyperplasia).
opsonins: Coatings that promote phagocytosis; the two major ones are IgG (Fc receptors) and C3b (complement receptors).
NETs: Neutrophil extracellular traps; webs of chromatin that snare extracellular microbes beyond the phagolysosome.
