hypochlorite: The most potent microbicide of oxygen-dependent killing, made by myeloperoxidase from H2O2.
Toll-like receptors (TLRs): Receptors recognizing conserved microbial patterns (e.g., LPS) to trigger inflammation.
serotonin: Preformed vasoactive amine stored in platelets; primarily a GI/CNS neurotransmitter with uncertain inflammatory role.
phospholipase A2: Rate-limiting enzyme freeing arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipid; blocked by corticosteroids.
cyclooxygenase (COX): Enzyme making prostaglandins and thromboxane from arachidonic acid; blocked by NSAIDs.
5-lipoxygenase (5-LOX): Enzyme making leukotrienes and lipoxins from arachidonic acid.
thromboxane A2 (TXA2): Platelet COX product driving aggregation and vasoconstriction.
LTC4/LTD4/LTE4: Cysteinyl leukotrienes causing bronchospasm and increased permeability (asthma).
lipoxins: Anti-inflammatory 5-LOX products that inhibit neutrophil recruitment and drive resolution.
corticosteroids: Anti-inflammatory drugs that block phospholipase A2, dropping BOTH prostaglandins and leukotrienes.
NSAIDs: Drugs blocking only COX, so prostaglandins fall but leukotrienes are spared.
chemokines: Small-cytokine subfamily whose defining job is chemotaxis (e.g., IL-8/CXCL8 for neutrophils).
IL-8 (CXCL8): Classic neutrophil chemokine; drives pus formation in abscess.
C3a and C5a: Anaphylatoxins that trigger mast-cell degranulation (C5a is also the neutrophil chemoattractant).
Factor XII: Hageman factor; activated by subendothelial collagen, it triggers coagulation, fibrinolysis, complement, and the kinin system.
serous inflammation: Cell-poor fluid effusion (e.g., a skin blister, early body-cavity effusion).
fibrinous inflammation: Eosinophilic fibrin-meshwork deposit on serosal surfaces (classic: bread-and-butter pericarditis).
suppurative inflammation: Neutrophil-rich purulent inflammation producing pus, made by pyogenic bacteria.
pus: Exudate of neutrophils, liquefied necrotic debris, and edema fluid.
ulcer: Surface excavation produced by sloughing of inflamed necrotic tissue.
chronic inflammation: Process with a mononuclear (macrophage/lymphocyte/plasma cell) infiltrate, tissue destruction, and fibrosis; from persistent infection, prolonged toxin, or autoimmunity.
mononuclear: The macrophage/lymphocyte/plasma-cell infiltrate that is the hallmark of chronic inflammation.
epithelioid: Activated macrophages with abundant pink cytoplasm forming the core of a granuloma.
caseating: Granuloma with central caseous necrosis (TB, fungal).
noncaseating: Granuloma without central necrosis (sarcoid, Crohn, foreign-body, cat-scratch); does NOT mean foreign-body.
sarcoidosis: Noncaseating granulomatous disease with no organism, CD4-driven, and bilateral hilar adenopathy.
hilar adenopathy: Bilateral mediastinal node enlargement classic for sarcoidosis.
cobblestone: The bowel-mucosa appearance of Crohn disease.
acid-fast: Staining property of mycobacteria; TB granulomas contain acid-fast bacilli.
gumma: The granulomatous lesion of tertiary syphilis.
SIRS: Systemic inflammatory response syndrome; the whole-body syndrome of high TNF (septic shock, DIC, metabolic failure).
regeneration: Repair restoring normal tissue; requires proliferative cells AND an intact connective-tissue framework.
scar formation: Repair by connective-tissue replacement (fibrosis) when the framework is destroyed or the tissue is permanent.
labile: Cells that divide continuously and fully regenerate (epidermis, GI mucosa, GU lining, bone marrow).
stable: Cells quiescent in G0 that divide when activated (liver, kidney, pancreas).
permanent: Terminally differentiated cells that cannot regenerate and heal by scar (neurons, cardiac muscle, skeletal muscle).
hepatectomy: Partial liver removal after which the stable hepatocytes regenerate remarkably (via IL-6 and HGF).
granulation tissue: Pink, soft, granular repair tissue of proliferating fibroblasts, new capillaries, and myofibroblasts.
VEGF: Vascular endothelial growth factor; drives angiogenesis by vessel sprouting.
Notch: Signaling pathway cross-talking with VEGF to control vessel spacing and branching in angiogenesis.
PDGF: Platelet-derived growth factor; drives fibroblast proliferation and chemotaxis.
myofibroblasts: Contractile repair cells in granulation tissue that mediate wound contraction.
lysyl oxidase: Copper-dependent enzyme that cross-links collagen for stability.
collagenase: Zinc-dependent matrix metalloproteinase that remodels scar by replacing type III with type I collagen.
first intention: Healing of a clean, well-apposed wound with minimal scar.
second intention: Healing of a large open wound with abundant granulation tissue and wound contraction.
hypertrophic scar: Excess scar staying WITHIN the original wound that may regress.
keloid: Excess scar growing BEYOND the original wound that does not regress; genetic predisposition, classically follows ear piercing.
fibrosis: Excessive collagen deposition in internal organs leading to dysfunction or failure; driven by TGF-beta.
edema: Excess interstitial fluid; a transudate from a Starling/pressure problem or an exudate from inflammation.
hydrostatic: Capillary pressure that, when raised (CHF, venous obstruction), drives fluid OUT into the interstitium.
colloid osmotic (oncotic): Plasma pull-back pressure (from albumin) whose fall lets fluid stay in tissue, causing transudate edema.
lymphedema: Edema from blocked lymphatic drainage (e.g., post-mastectomy arm, filariasis).
RAAS: Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system; activated in CHF to retain Na+ and water, worsening edema.
hyperemia: ACTIVE arteriolar dilation delivering oxygenated blood; tissue is red and warm.
congestion: PASSIVE impaired venous outflow backing up deoxygenated blood; tissue is cyanotic and cool.
nutmeg: The mottled liver appearance of chronic hepatic congestion (right heart failure).
heart-failure cells: Hemosiderin-laden alveolar macrophages of chronic pulmonary congestion (left heart failure).
vWF: Von Willebrand factor; bridges exposed collagen to platelet receptor GpIb for initial adhesion.
GpIb: Platelet receptor binding vWF in initial platelet ADHESION.
GpIIb/IIIa: Platelet receptor bridged by fibrinogen for platelet-to-platelet AGGREGATION.
fibrinogen: Soluble clotting protein that bridges platelet GpIIb/IIIa and is polymerized into fibrin; leaks to form alveolar hyaline membranes.
PTT: Partial thromboplastin time; measures the intrinsic pathway (factors VIII, IX, XI, XII).
antithrombin III: Anticoagulant inactivating factors IX, X, XI, XII and thrombin; potentiated by heparin.
heparin: Anticoagulant that potentiates antithrombin III; in HIT, antibodies to the heparin-PF4 complex cause clotting.
protein C: Anticoagulant that (with protein S) cleaves and inactivates factors Va and VIIIa.
protein S: Cofactor for protein C in inactivating factors Va and VIIIa.
Virchow's triad: The three determinants of thrombosis: endothelial injury (greatest influence), abnormal flow (stasis/turbulence), and hypercoagulability.
endothelial injury: The Virchow's-triad factor with the GREATEST influence on thrombosis.
hypercoagulability: A Virchow's-triad factor; a clotting-prone state (e.g., Factor V Leiden).
lines of Zahn: Alternating platelet/fibrin and RBC laminations proving a thrombus formed in FLOWING (antemortem) blood.
thrombus: An intravascular clot whose fates are propagation, embolization, dissolution, organization, and recanalization.
embolization: Detachment of a thrombus fragment that travels to lodge elsewhere.
recanalization: Re-establishment of blood flow through an organizing thrombus.
Factor V Leiden: The most common INHERITED hypercoagulable state, causing activated protein C (APC) resistance.
activated protein C (APC) resistance: The mechanism of Factor V Leiden, where factor V resists inactivation by protein C.
HIT: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia; antibodies to the heparin-PF4 complex activate platelets, so the patient CLOTS while the platelet count falls.
heparin-PF4 (platelet factor 4): The complex targeted by antibodies in HIT.
tissue factor: Trigger that fires the common coagulation pathway, initiating DIC microthrombi.
schistocytes: Fragmented RBCs formed as cells are sheared passing through microthrombi (seen in DIC).
saddle embolus: Pulmonary embolus lodged at the pulmonary-artery bifurcation, causing sudden death.
paradoxical: Embolus that crosses an ASD/PFO from the venous to systemic circulation, bypassing the lung filter.
ASD/PFO: Atrial septal defect / patent foramen ovale; the shunt allowing a paradoxical embolus.
red (hemorrhagic): Infarcts in dual-circulation, loose/spongy, or venous-occlusion tissues (classic: lung).
white (pale): Infarcts in end-arterial solid organs ('one way in'): heart, spleen, kidney.
end-arterial: Single-supply vascular pattern that yields pale (white) infarcts.
collaterals: Alternative vessels that open when occlusion develops slowly, limiting infarct severity.
SNP: Single-nucleotide polymorphism; a single-nucleotide variant present in >=1% of the population.
indel: A variant that adds or subtracts base pairs (typically 1 to ~10,000).
mitochondrial: Disorders that are always MATERNALLY inherited because the egg keeps its mtDNA at fertilization.
polygenic: Trait/disease determined by many genes plus environment, captured by an aggregate/polygenic risk score (not a single-gene test).
polygenic risk score: Aggregate score capturing risk from many variants for common, polygenic diseases.
ER/PR: Estrogen/progesterone receptor status; a breast-cancer treatment-selection marker independent of HER2.
Type I pneumocyte: Flat cell covering ~95% of the alveolar surface that carries out gas exchange.
Type II pneumocyte: Cuboidal cell that makes SURFACTANT and serves as the stem cell regenerating type I pneumocytes.
surfactant: Alveolar substance that lowers surface tension; DECREASED in pneumonia, contributing to alveolar collapse and poor gas exchange.
RSV: Respiratory syncytial virus; classic cause of bronchiolitis in infants under 1 year.
bronchiolitis: Small-airway inflammation in infants, classically from RSV.
interstitial: Pneumonia pattern with inflammation in the alveolar WALLS/interstitium (viral/Mycoplasma).
hyaline membranes: Leaked plasma fibrinogen polymerized into fibrin across a damaged alveolar wall; a feature of diffuse alveolar damage/ARDS.
diffuse alveolar damage (DAD): The morphology of ARDS: type I pneumocyte death + type II hyperplasia + hyaline membranes.
ARDS: Acute respiratory distress syndrome; clinically corresponds to diffuse alveolar damage.
apoptosis: Programmed cell death keeping the membrane INTACT with NO inflammation; cell shrinkage, chromatin condensation, and apoptotic bodies.
apoptotic bodies: Membrane-bound fragments shed by an apoptotic cell.
BAX/BAK: Pro-apoptotic proteins forming mitochondrial pores that release cytochrome c (intrinsic pathway).
cytochrome c: Mitochondrial protein released through BAX/BAK pores to activate caspase-9 in intrinsic apoptosis.
FasL-Fas: Death-receptor pair engaging FADD to activate caspase-8 in extrinsic apoptosis.
FADD: Adapter recruited by Fas to activate caspase-8 in extrinsic apoptosis.
caspase: Executioner protease (e.g., caspase-3/6) onto which both apoptotic pathways converge.
necroptosis: Programmed but caspase-INDEPENDENT death (RIPK1/RIPK3 then MLKL pores) ending in rupture and inflammation.
dystrophic: Pathologic calcification in DAMAGED tissue with NORMAL serum calcium (e.g., degenerating aortic valve).
metastatic calcification: Calcification of NORMAL tissue from HIGH serum calcium (hyperparathyroidism, bone destruction, vitamin D excess, renal failure).
steatosis: Fatty change; in alcoholic liver, ethanol raises NADH and blocks lipid export so triglyceride fills the hepatocyte (clear vacuole on H&E).
NADH: Reduced cofactor raised by ethanol metabolism, favoring lipid synthesis in alcoholic steatosis.
A1AT deficiency: Alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency; misfolded protein trapped in the LIVER, with loss of anti-elastase letting neutrophil elastase destroy alveoli (emphysema).
elastase: Neutrophil enzyme that destroys alveolar walls when unopposed in A1AT deficiency.
emphysema: Destruction of alveolar walls (e.g., from unopposed elastase in A1AT deficiency).
hypertrophy: Increase in cell SIZE from synthesizing more structural protein; how permanent cells (cardiac/skeletal muscle) adapt to load.
BPH: Benign prostatic hyperplasia; treated with alpha-1 antagonists (-osin); worsened by antimuscarinics (urinary retention).
intracellular accumulations: Reversible buildup of material from abnormal metabolism, a folding/transport defect, a missing enzyme, or indigestible material.
Pharmacodynamics: The study of what the DRUG does to the BODY (receptor binding, dose-response, efficacy, potency). Contrast with pharmacokinetics.
Pharmacokinetics: The study of what the BODY does to the DRUG: absorption, distribution, metabolism, elimination (ADME).
ADME: The four steps of pharmacokinetics: Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, Elimination.
ADH: Antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin). Relevant here because demeclocycline inhibits renal ADH activity to treat SIADH.
SIADH: Syndrome of Inappropriate ADH secretion, causing chronic hyponatremia; treated with demeclocycline (blocks renal ADH).
first-pass: First-pass (hepatic) metabolism: oral drug is partly metabolized in the liver before reaching systemic circulation, LOWERING oral bioavailability.
first-pass metabolism: Metabolism of an orally absorbed drug in the liver (via the portal vein) before it reaches systemic circulation; reduces oral bioavailability.
portal vein: Vessel carrying orally absorbed drug from gut to liver, where first-pass metabolism occurs before the drug reaches systemic circulation.
bioavailability: Fraction (F) of an administered dose reaching systemic circulation unchanged. IV = 100%; oral is lower due to incomplete absorption and first-pass metabolism. F = AUC(oral)/AUC(IV).
oral bioavailability: Fraction of an oral dose reaching the systemic circulation; below 100% due to incomplete absorption and first-pass metabolism.
bioequivalent: Two formulations whose RATE and EXTENT of absorption are not significantly different (comparable bioavailability and time-to-peak).
bioequivalence: Comparable rate and extent of absorption between two formulations; required (with pharmaceutical equivalence) for therapeutic equivalence.
pharmaceutical equivalence: Same dosage form, active ingredient, strength, and route. Combined with bioequivalence it gives therapeutic equivalence.
AUC: Area Under the Curve of plasma concentration vs time; used to compute bioavailability (F = AUC oral / AUC IV).
volume of distribution: Vd = amount of drug in body / plasma concentration. HIGH Vd = extensive tissue distribution (lipophilic drugs); LOW Vd = stays in plasma (hydrophilic or highly protein-bound).
clearance: Volume of plasma cleared of drug per unit time. CL = Vd x Ke (where Ke = 0.693/half-life). Total clearance is the sum of all elimination routes; reduced clearance causes accumulation.
half-life: Time for plasma concentration to fall by 50% during elimination. After 5 half-lives ~95-98% is eliminated; steady state on repeated dosing in ~4-5 half-lives.
first-order: Kinetics removing a constant PERCENTAGE/FRACTION of drug per unit time, giving exponential decline and a constant half-life. Most drugs.
zero-order: Kinetics removing a constant AMOUNT of drug per unit time, giving linear decline and no true half-life. Only phenytoin and high-dose aspirin (warfarin is FIRST-order).
loading: Loading dose = a high initial dose to reach target concentration fast. Loading dose = Vd x desired Css / F.
maintenance: Maintenance dose: given after loading to sustain a steady-state level in the therapeutic window; replaces only drug lost to metabolism and excretion.
therapeutic window: Concentration range high enough for efficacy but below toxicity. Dosing keeps the level inside it between doses.
therapeutic index: TI = TD50 / ED50 (or LD50/ED50 in animals). A WIDER index means a SAFER drug.
ED50: Median EFFECTIVE dose: dose producing the desired effect in 50% of a population. Denominator of therapeutic index.
TD50: Median TOXIC dose: dose producing toxicity in 50% of a population (human endpoint). Numerator of therapeutic index.
LD50: Median LETHAL dose (an ANIMAL-study term); the human equivalent endpoint is TD50.
EC50: Concentration producing 50% of maximal effect; indexes POTENCY (read off the x-axis). Lower EC50 = more potent (left-shifted curve).
Emax: Maximal effect a drug can produce; indexes EFFICACY (read off the plateau/y-axis). Reached when all responsive receptors are occupied.
potency: The dose/concentration needed for a given effect, indexed by EC50. A more potent drug is left-shifted. Independent of efficacy; clinically less important than efficacy.
efficacy: The MAXIMAL effect a drug can achieve (Emax). Independent of potency; clinically outranks potency.
intrinsic activity: The ability of a bound drug to produce a response. Order: full agonist > partial > antagonist (zero) > inverse (negative). Affinity gets the drug on; intrinsic activity decides the effect.
agonist: A drug that occupies a receptor and PRODUCES the response (has intrinsic activity).
antagonist: A drug that occupies a receptor and BLOCKS the endogenous ligand, with NO intrinsic activity of its own.
partial: Partial agonist: has affinity but LOWER intrinsic activity, giving a submaximal response even at full receptor saturation (e.g. varenicline, pindolol, buprenorphine).
inverse: Inverse agonist: has NEGATIVE intrinsic activity, driving response BELOW baseline by stabilizing the inactive receptor (e.g. chlorpheniramine at H1).
competitive: Competitive antagonist: binds reversibly at the SAME site; shifts the dose-response curve RIGHT (lower potency) with Emax unchanged (surmountable).
non-competitive: Non-competitive antagonist: binds irreversibly/allosterically; LOWERS Emax and cannot be overcome by more agonist (insurmountable).
receptor: A protein (enzyme, transporter, ion channel, or surface protein) that binds a ligand to alter cell function; the drug's site of action.
site of action: The receptor where the drug-receptor complex forms and the response begins.
ligand: The molecule (endogenous or drug) that binds a receptor. An 'orphan receptor' has an unknown natural ligand.
spare receptor: Reserve receptors; a full agonist can reach Emax while occupying only a small fraction of total receptors.
GPCR: G-protein-coupled receptor: the MOST ABUNDANT receptor class, with SEVEN transmembrane domains; signals via G-alpha (GDP->GTP exchange) and second messengers like cAMP.
G-alpha: The G-protein subunit that undergoes GDP->GTP exchange on agonist binding, then dissociates from beta-gamma to activate an effector (e.g. adenylyl cyclase).
adenylyl cyclase: Effector enzyme generating cAMP. Stimulated by Gs, inhibited by Gi.
cAMP: Cyclic AMP, the classic GPCR second messenger made by adenylyl cyclase. Raised by Gs, lowered by Gi.
Gs-protein: Stimulatory G-protein: stimulates adenylyl cyclase, RAISING cAMP. All beta-adrenergic receptors couple to Gs.
Gi-protein: Inhibitory G-protein: inhibits adenylyl cyclase, LOWERING cAMP (e.g. slows the heart). Even-numbered muscarinics (M2, M4) and alpha-2 couple to Gi.
Gq-protein: G-protein activating phospholipase C -> IP3 -> calcium release. Odd-numbered muscarinics (M1, M3, M5) and alpha-1 couple to Gq.
phospholipase C: Gq-activated effector enzyme that generates IP3 (and DAG).
IP3: Inositol trisphosphate; second messenger made by phospholipase C that triggers calcium release from the endoplasmic reticulum.
RTK: Receptor tyrosine kinase: responds to ligand by autophosphorylation of tyrosine residues; overstimulation (e.g. EGFR) drives cancer.
autophosphorylation: Self-phosphorylation of tyrosine residues on a receptor tyrosine kinase's cytosolic domain upon ligand binding.
transcription factor: Role of activated nuclear/intracellular receptors; requires a lipophilic drug to cross the membrane, giving slow-onset, long-duration effects.
tachyphylaxis: Rapid reduction in drug response within minutes of repeated dosing.
desensitization: Loss of response from receptor phosphorylation plus internalization/downregulation (fewer surface receptors); e.g. albuterol desensitizing beta-adrenergic receptors.
internalization: Endocytosis of receptors that, with phosphorylation/downregulation, produces desensitization.
upregulation: Increase in receptor number causing increased sensitivity (sensitization); e.g. chronic haloperidol upregulating dopamine receptors.
passive diffusion: Membrane transport needing NO energy and NO carrier, moving drug DOWN its gradient; cannot be saturated or inhibited (e.g. aspirin, ethanol, diazepam).
facilitated diffusion: Carrier-mediated transport that needs NO ATP and runs WITH the concentration gradient (e.g. glucose via GLUT).
active transport: Carrier-mediated transport that requires ATP and moves drug AGAINST its gradient; saturable and inhibitable (e.g. L-dopa via the amino-acid carrier).
endocytosis: Vesicle engulfment used to bring large molecules (insulin, vitamin B12, peptides) into cells.
P-glycoprotein: An ATP-dependent EFFLUX pump that throws drug back out of the cell, causing cancer drug resistance.
ionized: Charged, water-soluble drug form that is TRAPPED in the renal tubule and EXCRETED. Weak acids ionize in alkaline urine; weak bases ionize in acidic urine.
non-ionized: Uncharged, lipid-soluble drug form that is ABSORBED (and reabsorbed in the tubule).
un-ionized: Uncharged, lipophilic drug form that is absorbed across membranes and REABSORBED in the renal tubule.
free fraction: The unbound portion of drug; only free drug is active and can distribute, be metabolized, and be filtered. Low albumin raises free fraction.
free drug: Unbound drug; the only form that is pharmacologically active and available for distribution, metabolism, and renal filtration.
Phase I: Metabolism by oxidation, reduction, or hydrolysis (via CYP450) that unmasks a polar group.
Phase II: Metabolism by conjugation (e.g. glucuronidation) that makes a drug water-soluble for excretion.
conjugation: Phase II metabolism (e.g. glucuronidation) adding a polar group to make the drug water-soluble for excretion.
glucuronidation: A Phase II conjugation reaction; deficient in neonates (lack glucuronosyltransferase), explaining gray baby syndrome with chloramphenicol.
CYP: Cytochrome P450 enzymes performing Phase I metabolism. Inducers speed metabolism (lower drug levels); inhibitors slow it (raise levels/toxicity).
CYP450: Cytochrome P450 enzyme system for Phase I drug metabolism; central to many drug interactions (induction vs inhibition).
CYP3A4: A major cytochrome P450 isoenzyme. Inhibited by azoles and macrolides; substrates include oxybutynin, silodosin, and alfuzosin.
CYP2D6: Cytochrome P450 isoenzyme inhibited by mirabegron (raising metoprolol and digoxin levels).
induction: CYP induction: speeds substrate metabolism, LOWERING its level (may need a higher dose). Inducers: rifampin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital.
redistribution: Termination of drug effect by the drug leaving the brain for muscle/fat (e.g. thiopental, propofol), ending action BEFORE elimination.
blood-brain barrier: Tight endothelial junctions that admit small LIPOPHILIC drugs and block hydrophilic ones; bypassed by intrathecal injection.
muscarinic: Cholinergic GPCR subtype (M1-M5) for ACh. Odd (M1,M3,M5)=Gq/excitatory; even (M2,M4)=Gi/inhibitory.
nicotinic: Cholinergic LIGAND-GATED ion channel (Na+/K+). NN on autonomic ganglia and adrenal medulla; NM at the skeletal NMJ. Needs two ACh to open.
M1 receptor: Muscarinic subtype (Gq, excitatory) in the CNS, autonomic ganglia, and gastric/exocrine glands; central block gives sedation->confusion. Striatal M1 is blocked by antiparkinsonian antimuscarinics.
M2 receptor: Cardiac muscarinic subtype (Gi, inhibitory); activation causes BRADYCARDIA. Blockade (antimuscarinic) causes tachycardia from lost vagal tone.
M3 receptor: Default peripheral non-cardiac muscarinic subtype (Gq): glands, bronchi, GI/bladder smooth muscle, iris sphincter. Bronchial M3 tone constricts airways.
NN receptor: Neuronal nicotinic receptor on autonomic GANGLIA and the adrenal medulla.
NM receptor: Muscle-type nicotinic receptor at the skeletal NEUROMUSCULAR JUNCTION (NMJ).
NMJ: Neuromuscular junction; site of NM nicotinic receptors. Sustained nicotinic activation here causes depolarizing block (paralysis).
ACh: Acetylcholine; the neurotransmitter at all preganglionic fibers, postganglionic parasympathetic fibers, sympathetic fibers to sweat glands, and the NMJ.
acetylcholine: The cholinergic neurotransmitter; used pharmacologically to induce surgical miosis. Synthesized by ChAT, hydrolyzed by AChE.
acetylcholinesterase: AChE: enzyme that hydrolyzes ACh into choline + acetate in microseconds. Target of indirect cholinergic agonists and organophosphates.
AChE: Acetylcholinesterase; hydrolyzes ACh. Inhibited (reversibly) by carbamates and (irreversibly) by organophosphates.
ChAT: Choline acetyltransferase; synthesizes ACh from choline + acetyl-CoA.
DUMB BELLS: Mnemonic for parasympathetic/muscarinic over-activation (Diarrhea, Urination, Miosis, Bradycardia/Bronchospasm, Emesis, Lacrimation, Lethargy, Salivation).
SLUDGE-MB: Muscarinic toxidrome mnemonic (Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defecation, GI distress, Emesis, Miosis, Bronchospasm/Bradycardia).
MATCH: Nicotinic component of cholinergic crisis (Muscle weakness/cramps, Adrenal/sympathetic stimulation, Tachycardia, Cramps, Hypertension/Hyperglycemia).
RLSC: CNS component of cholinergic crisis (Respiratory depression, Lethargy, Seizures, Coma).
muscarine: Mushroom toxin and direct muscarinic agonist resisting AChE because it has NO ester bond; toxicity treated with atropine (give oxygen first).
carbachol: Direct cholinergic agonist activating BOTH muscarinic AND nicotinic receptors; reserved largely for topical ocular use (glaucoma).
bethanechol: Muscarinic-only direct agonist acting on bladder and bowel; used for urinary retention.
methacholine: Muscarinic-selective direct agonist used in the bronchial challenge (asthma) test.
pilocarpine: Tertiary-amine muscarinic agonist that CROSSES into the CNS; treats glaucoma and dry mouth (xerostomia).
cevimeline: M3-SELECTIVE, oral muscarinic agonist for dry mouth (xerostomia), with fewer side effects than pilocarpine.
varenicline: Alpha4-beta2 nicotinic PARTIAL agonist used for smoking cessation.
physostigmine: TERTIARY carbamate AChE inhibitor that reaches the CNS; antidote for atropine/antimuscarinic toxicity (reverses central and peripheral effects).
neostigmine: QUATERNARY carbamate AChE inhibitor (peripheral) with added direct NICOTINIC (NMJ) action; treats myasthenia gravis and reverses nondepolarizing block.
pyridostigmine: Quaternary carbamate AChE inhibitor for chronic ORAL myasthenia gravis and nerve-agent PRETREATMENT (for soman).
carbamate: Class of REVERSIBLE AChE inhibitors (the '-stigmine' drugs); carbamylate the AChE serine with slow hydrolysis.
organophosphate: IRREVERSIBLE AChE inhibitors that phosphorylate the AChE serine; bond strengthens over time ('aging'), then permanent. Treated with atropine + 2-PAM + benzodiazepine.
aging: Strengthening of the organophosphate-AChE bond over time, after which inhibition is PERMANENT and 2-PAM no longer works.
2-PAM: Pralidoxime; reactivates organophosphate-inhibited AChE but ONLY before aging. Quaternary, so peripheral only (no CNS effect).
pralidoxime: 2-PAM; an oxime that reactivates organophosphate-poisoned AChE before aging occurs; acts peripherally (does not treat CNS symptoms).
soman: A nerve agent (organophosphate); pyridostigmine is the pretreatment given BEFORE exposure.
succinylcholine: Depolarizing neuromuscular blocker; its block is PROLONGED by AChE inhibitors (major drug interaction).
depolarizing block: Paralysis from sustained nicotinic activation holding the membrane depolarized so it cannot repolarize and refire.
atropine: Tertiary-amine antimuscarinic (crosses BBB); antidote for organophosphate/muscarinic poisoning, first-line for symptomatic sinus bradycardia, pre-op drying, and mydriasis.
scopolamine: Tertiary antimuscarinic crossing the BBB even more than atropine; drug of choice for MOTION SICKNESS (transdermal patch).
ipratropium: Short-acting muscarinic antagonist (SAMA), dosed four times daily, for COPD MAINTENANCE (not acute attacks).
tiotropium: Once-daily, functionally M3-selective long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA); the COPD benchmark.
SAMA: Short-Acting Muscarinic Antagonist (e.g. ipratropium); inhaled maintenance bronchodilator.
LAMA: Long-Acting Muscarinic Antagonist (e.g. tiotropium); once/twice-daily inhaled COPD maintenance.
glycopyrrolate: Twice-daily LAMA; its named DDI is with oral potassium chloride (slowed GI transit prolongs KCl mucosal contact).
trospium: QUATERNARY bladder antimuscarinic that stays OUT of the brain; preferred for overactive bladder in Parkinson or Alzheimer patients.
darifenacin: Bladder antimuscarinic with the HIGHEST M3 selectivity.
oxybutynin: Bladder antimuscarinic; a CYP3A4 substrate. Transdermal patch/gel cuts systemic anticholinergic effects.
tolterodine: Bladder antimuscarinic with LESS dry mouth than oxybutynin.
tropicamide: Ocular antimuscarinic with ~3-hour duration (quick fundus exam).
cyclopentolate: Ocular antimuscarinic lasting ~12-24 hours; carries pediatric CNS risk (drowsiness, hallucinations) from systemic absorption.
benztropine: Antimuscarinic blocking striatal M1 receptors; treats Parkinson tremor/rigidity (adjunct) and antipsychotic-induced extrapyramidal symptoms.
hexamethonium: Ganglionic blocker acting at NICOTINIC NN receptors; lack of autonomic selectivity makes ganglionic blockers rarely used therapeutically.
isoproterenol: Nonselective beta agonist (top of the beta-affinity ladder); CONTRAINDICATED in shock because beta-2 vasodilation worsens hypotension.
norepinephrine: Alpha-1 >> beta catecholamine (minimal beta-2); pressor for septic/neurogenic shock. Extravasation -> necrosis (treat with phentolamine).
dobutamine: Predominantly BETA-1 agonist (inotropy > chronotropy) with NO dopamine-receptor activity; used for cardiogenic shock.
dopamine: Catecholamine with a dose ladder: low = D1 (renal/mesenteric vasodilation), mid = beta-1, high = alpha-1 (vasoconstriction). Also a central neurotransmitter.
phenylephrine: Selective alpha-1 agonist; pressor, terminates paroxysmal SVT via reflex bradycardia, gives mydriasis WITHOUT cycloplegia.
albuterol: Short-acting beta-2 agonist (SABA) bronchodilator for acute asthma relief; example of beta-receptor desensitization.
salmeterol: Long-acting beta-2 agonist (LABA) with SLOW onset (not for acute relief); must be paired with an inhaled corticosteroid.
formoterol: Long-acting beta-2 agonist with FASTER onset than salmeterol; still requires pairing with an inhaled corticosteroid.
mirabegron: Beta-3 agonist for overactive bladder; adverse effects include hypertension and CYP2D6 inhibition (raises metoprolol, digoxin).
clonidine: Central ALPHA-2 sympatholytic antihypertensive; never stop abruptly (rebound hypertension).
oxymetazoline: Topical alpha agonist decongestant; overuse beyond 3 days causes rebound congestion; large doses cause central alpha-2 (clonidine-like) hypotension.
ICS: Inhaled corticosteroid; the anti-inflammatory controller that any LABA (-terol) MUST be paired with in asthma, because LABA monotherapy raises asthma-related death.
amphetamine: Indirect sympathomimetic that runs NET/DAT BACKWARD (reverse transport), expelling NE/DA; high abuse potential. Toxicity treated with chlorpromazine.
methylphenidate: Indirect sympathomimetic that only BLOCKS reuptake (no reverse transport); lower abuse potential; ADHD; gives CNS stimulation without increased motor activity.
cocaine: Indirect sympathomimetic blocking reuptake; one legitimate use as a LOCAL ANESTHETIC (independently blocks neuronal action potentials).
atomoxetine: NON-stimulant ADHD drug; a selective NE-reuptake inhibitor; not habit-forming and NOT a controlled substance.
tyramine: Dietary amine loaded into vesicles by VMAT that displaces NE; with an MAOI it triggers the 'cheese reaction' hypertensive crisis.
cheese reaction: MAOI hypertensive crisis: blocked MAO lets dietary tyramine reach the neuron, load into vesicles via VMAT, and dump a surge of NE.
lisdexamfetamine: Amphetamine PRODRUG (~12 h duration); first FDA-approved for binge-eating disorder; explicitly NOT for weight loss; Schedule II.
ephedrine: MIXED-ACTION sympathomimetic (releases NE AND acts directly on alpha/beta); MAO-resistant; contraindicated within 14 days of an MAOI.
VMAT: Vesicular monoamine transporter; loads monoamines (including tyramine) into synaptic vesicles. Displacement of NE is one indirect mechanism.
MAO: Monoamine oxidase; degrades catecholamines and dietary tyramine. Inhibition (MAOI) risks hypertensive crisis with sympathomimetics/tyramine.
MAOI: Monoamine oxidase inhibitor; blocks catecholamine/tyramine breakdown, risking hypertensive crisis ('cheese reaction') with indirect sympathomimetics.
PNMT: Phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase; converts NE -> epinephrine, ONLY in the adrenal medulla.
tyrosine hydroxylase: Rate-limiting enzyme of catecholamine synthesis, converting tyrosine -> L-DOPA.
phenoxybenzamine: NONSELECTIVE alpha-blocker binding COVALENTLY (noncompetitive, irreversible, long-acting); pre-op drug of choice in pheochromocytoma.
phentolamine: Nonselective, COMPETITIVE/REVERSIBLE, short-acting alpha-blocker; rescue for NE-extravasation necrosis and states of alpha-1 excess; acute pheochromocytoma.
prazosin: Selective alpha-1 antagonist (-osin) blocking alpha-1A + alpha-1B; treats BPH AND hypertension; first-dose orthostatic hypotension.
tamsulosin: Alpha-1A-SELECTIVE antagonist; BPH-only (BP spared); most associated with intraoperative floppy iris syndrome.
silodosin: Alpha-1A-selective antagonist; BPH-only; notable for reversible retrograde ejaculation; contraindicated in severe renal impairment; CYP3A4 substrate.
alfuzosin: Alpha-1A-selective antagonist; BPH-only; cautioned with QT-prolongation risk; CYP3A4 substrate.
doxazosin: Alpha-1 antagonist (blocks 1A+1B) for BPH and hypertension; specific risk of hepatitis and angioedema.
olol: Drug-name suffix marking a beta-blocker (e.g. propranolol, metoprolol).
labetalol: MIXED alpha/beta blocker (no -olol suffix); owns gestational hypertension/preeclampsia and hypertensive emergencies; specifically hepatotoxic.
carvedilol: MIXED alpha/beta blocker (no -olol suffix); reduces heart-failure mortality; adds alpha-1 vasodilation plus antioxidant/anti-remodeling effects.
propranolol: Prototype NONSELECTIVE beta-blocker (beta-1 = beta-2), no ISA, highly lipophilic; dangerous in insulin-treated diabetics (masks hypoglycemia, blocks glycogenolysis).
metoprolol: Cardioselective (beta-1) blocker; reduces heart-failure mortality; poorly CNS-penetrant.
atenolol: Cardioselective (beta-1) blocker; poorly CNS-penetrant (lacks propranolol's central effects).
esmolol: Cardioselective ULTRA-SHORT-ACTING beta-1 blocker for emergencies.
nebivolol: Beta-1-selective blocker that uniquely causes vasodilation by stimulating endothelial NITRIC OXIDE release.
bisoprolol: Cardioselective (beta-1) blocker; one of the heart-failure mortality-reducing beta-blockers.
timolol: Nonselective beta-blocker WITHOUT ISA; used topically for glaucoma.
pindolol: Nonselective beta-blocker WITH intrinsic sympathomimetic activity (ISA); partial agonist used when cardiac reserve is diminished.
acebutolol: Cardioselective beta-blocker WITH ISA; box warning never to stop abruptly (taper over 1-2 weeks).
ISA: Intrinsic sympathomimetic activity; partial beta-agonism (pindolol, penbutolol, acebutolol). Timolol and nadolol lack it.
nitric oxide: NO; endothelial vasodilator whose release nebivolol uniquely stimulates.
ICS-LABA: Inhaled corticosteroid plus long-acting beta agonist; LABA must never be used as monotherapy in asthma.
RIPE: Mnemonic for first-line anti-TB drugs: Rifampin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol.
isoniazid: First-line anti-TB cornerstone; activated by mycobacterial catalase-peroxidase; inhibits MYCOLIC-ACID synthesis. Toxicities: hepatotoxicity and peripheral neuropathy (give B6).
rifampin: Bactericidal anti-TB drug inhibiting DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (rpoB); turns secretions red-orange; STRONG CYP inducer; contraindicated with HIV protease inhibitors.
pyrazinamide: First-line anti-TB drug activated by mycobacterial pyrazinamidase; given only the first 2 of 6 months; toxicities: hepatotoxicity and hyperuricemia.
ethambutol: First-line anti-TB drug blocking arabinosyl transferase (arabinogalactan synthesis); signature toxicity is retrobulbar optic neuritis (red-green color blindness).
rifabutin: Rifamycin substituted for rifampin when an HIV protease inhibitor is required.
mycolic acid: Very long-chain (C60-C90) lipids giving mycobacteria their acid-fast wall; synthesis inhibited by isoniazid.
rpoB: The RNA polymerase subunit targeted by rifampin; mutations confer resistance.
DOT: Direct Observation Therapy; watching the patient swallow each TB dose to ensure adherence.
MDR-TB: Multidrug-resistant TB: resistance to at least isoniazid + rifampin.
XDR-TB: Extensively drug-resistant TB: MDR-TB plus resistance to key second-line agents.
pyridoxine: Vitamin B6; co-administered with isoniazid to prevent peripheral neuropathy.
dapsone: Folate-synthesis inhibitor; first-line for leprosy and used for Pneumocystis (PCP) prophylaxis in AIDS; NOT for atypical mycobacteria; causes hemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
clofazimine: Anti-leprosy drug (DNA binding) that causes skin discoloration.
beta-lactam: Antibiotic class defined by the beta-lactam ring; bind PBPs (transpeptidases) to block peptidoglycan cross-linking; cleaved/inactivated by beta-lactamase.
beta-lactamase: Bacterial enzyme that cleaves the beta-lactam ring, inactivating penicillins/cephalosporins; overcome by inhibitors like clavulanate, sulbactam, tazobactam.
PBP: Penicillin-binding protein (transpeptidase) that cross-links peptidoglycan; the target of beta-lactams. Altered PBP2a confers MRSA resistance.
PBP2a: Altered penicillin-binding protein in MRSA that beta-lactams cannot bind, conferring resistance; covered instead by vancomycin or ceftaroline.
autolysin: Bacterial enzyme activated by penicillins, contributing to their BACTERICIDAL effect (beyond blocking cross-linking).
penicilloic acid: The penicillin metabolite that drives hypersensitivity reactions (up to Stevens-Johnson and anaphylaxis).
penicillin G: Drug of choice for syphilis (T. pallidum) with essentially no resistance; ionized so fails in the prostate.
benzathine penicillin G: Long-acting IM depot penicillin holding effective levels up to a week; the syphilis regimen (2.4 million units IM).
amoxicillin: Oral aminopenicillin workhorse and endocarditis prophylaxis agent; acid-stable but NOT penicillinase-resistant.
ampicillin: Aminopenicillin; drug of choice for Listeria; highest incidence of rash among penicillins; not penicillinase-resistant.
nafcillin: IV antistaphylococcal (penicillinase-resistant) penicillin covering MSSA only.
oxacillin: Oral antistaphylococcal (penicillinase-resistant) penicillin covering MSSA only.
piperacillin: Most potent antipseudomonal penicillin; with tazobactam (Zosyn) treats serious nosocomial polymicrobial Pseudomonas infections.
clavulanate: A beta-lactamase inhibitor combined with amoxicillin (Augmentin).
MSSA: Methicillin-SENSITIVE Staphylococcus aureus; covered by antistaphylococcal penicillins (nafcillin, oxacillin, dicloxacillin).
imipenem: Broad-spectrum carbapenem given with cilastatin (blocks renal dehydropeptidase); seizure risk at high levels in renal impairment.
meropenem: Broad-spectrum carbapenem; LESS seizure-prone than imipenem.
cilastatin: Inhibitor of renal dehydropeptidase co-formulated with imipenem to prevent a nephrotoxic metabolite.
dehydropeptidase: Renal enzyme that degrades imipenem to a nephrotoxic metabolite; inhibited by cilastatin.
aztreonam: The lone MONOBACTAM; covers gram-NEGATIVE rods only (incl. Pseudomonas); no cross-reactivity with penicillins (safe in penicillin allergy).
monobactam: Beta-lactam class with a single ring (aztreonam); gram-negative-only, safe in penicillin allergy.
carbapenem: Broadest-spectrum beta-lactams (but NOT MRSA); includes imipenem (with cilastatin) and meropenem.
cephalosporin: Beta-lactam class; up the generations gram-positive coverage falls while gram-negative coverage and CNS penetration rise.
ceftriaxone: 3rd-generation cephalosporin; first-line for gonorrhea (500 mg IM) and bacterial meningitis.
cefazolin: 1st-generation cephalosporin; drug of choice for surgical prophylaxis.
MTT: Methylthiotetrazole side chain (cefotetan, cefamandole, cefoperazone) causing bleeding (anti-vitamin K) and a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol.
vancomycin: Glycopeptide binding D-Ala-D-Ala (the cell-wall SUBSTRATE, not the PBP); covers MRSA. IV for systemic infection, ORAL for C. difficile colitis.
D-Ala-D-Ala: The cell-wall building-block terminus that vancomycin binds, blocking cross-linking; dodges beta-lactamase/altered-PBP resistance.
red-man syndrome: Rate-dependent histamine release from vancomycin (NOT an IgE allergy); managed by slowing the infusion.
fosfomycin: Cell-wall inhibitor blocking enolpyruvate transferase (MurA); single 3 g oral dose for uncomplicated UTI; safe in pregnancy.
bacitracin: Cell-wall synthesis inhibitor used TOPICALLY only (systemically nephrotoxic); a component of triple-antibiotic ointment.
polymyxin: Cationic detergent disrupting the gram-negative LPS/phospholipid membrane; gram-negative-only; nephrotoxic and neurotoxic.
colistin: Polymyxin E; revived as IV salvage therapy for multidrug-resistant gram-negatives despite nephro/neurotoxicity.
cycloserine: D-alanine analog inhibiting alanine racemase + D-Ala ligase; only cell-wall inhibitor used in TB (second-line); CNS toxicity (psychosis, convulsions).
daptomycin: Lipopeptide that depolarizes the membrane to treat MRSA/VRE bacteremia; INACTIVATED by pulmonary surfactant so NEVER used for pneumonia; monitor CPK.
telavancin: Lipoglycopeptide that DOES treat MRSA HABP/VABP; contraindicated in pregnancy.
tetracycline: Bacteriostatic, broad-spectrum 30S-binding (reversible) antibiotic; chelated by dairy/antacids/iron; deposits in bone and teeth (avoid in children/pregnancy).
doxycycline: Tetracycline eliminated by BILE (safe in renal failure); first-line for Lyme disease and Rocky Mountain spotted fever; penicillin-allergy syphilis option.
minocycline: Tetracycline that concentrates in ear endolymph, causing distinctive VESTIBULAR toxicity (dizziness, vertigo, tinnitus).
demeclocycline: Tetracycline that treats SIADH-related chronic hyponatremia by inhibiting renal ADH activity.
tigecycline: Glycylcycline (tetracycline derivative) with signature acute pancreatitis (boxed warning), IV only.
macrolide: 50S-binding bacteriostatic antibiotics blocking TRANSLOCATION; class liabilities are CYP3A4 inhibition and QT prolongation.
erythromycin: Macrolide; worst GI upset (motilin agonist); highest QT prolongation; signature toxicity acute cholestatic hepatitis.
azithromycin: Macrolide with a LONG half-life (single-dose regimens); first-line for community-acquired pneumonia (Z-pack); minor CYP3A4 inhibitor; avoid in myasthenia gravis.
clarithromycin: Macrolide used in H. pylori triple therapy; a STRONG CYP3A4 inhibitor.
aminoglycoside: Bactericidal 30S(16S)-binding antibiotics with OXYGEN-DEPENDENT uptake (useless vs anaerobes); concentration-dependent killing (once-daily); nephro/oto/neuromuscular toxicity.
gentamicin: Gram-negative workhorse aminoglycoside; used for endocarditis synergy; among the most nephrotoxic.
amikacin: Aminoglycoside that resists most modifying enzymes (multidrug-resistant niche); second-line anti-mycobacterial.
streptomycin: Aminoglycoside used as a second-line anti-mycobacterial agent.
neomycin: Aminoglycoside restricted to topical/oral use (too toxic parenterally); among the most nephrotoxic; in triple-antibiotic ointment.
ototoxicity: Aminoglycoside-induced death of cochlear/vestibular hair cells; often IRREVERSIBLE (hair cells do not regenerate); worsened by loop diuretics.
nephrotoxicity: Aminoglycoside-induced acute tubular necrosis; usually REVERSIBLE (tubular cells regenerate); worsened by vancomycin, amphotericin B, cisplatin.
post-antibiotic: Post-antibiotic effect: continued bacterial suppression after drug levels fall (aminoglycosides), justifying extended-interval dosing.
spectinomycin: Aminocyclitol (related to aminoglycosides) binding the 30S subunit; single 2 g IM dose for gonorrhea in penicillin-allergic/resistant cases.
chloramphenicol: 50S peptidyl-transferase inhibitor; last-resort due to dose-INDEPENDENT aplastic anemia and neonatal gray baby syndrome; inhibits CYP (raises phenytoin/warfarin).
gray baby syndrome: Chloramphenicol toxicity in neonates who lack hepatic glucuronosyltransferase, so the drug accumulates.
aplastic anemia: Rare, dose-INDEPENDENT, often fatal blood toxicity of chloramphenicol.
clindamycin: Lincosamide binding 50S, blocking chain elongation; covers gram-positive cocci plus anaerobes (above the diaphragm); signature C. difficile colitis.
lincosamide: Antibiotic class (clindamycin) binding the 50S subunit and blocking chain elongation.
linezolid: Oxazolidinone binding 23S rRNA, blocking the 70S initiation complex; covers VRE and MRSA; oral and IV; weak MAO inhibitor (serotonin syndrome risk); thrombocytopenia.
oxazolidinone: Antibiotic class (linezolid, tedizolid) binding 23S rRNA to block the 70S initiation complex; little cross-resistance; for resistant gram-positives.
tedizolid: Newer oxazolidinone marketed for complicated skin and skin-structure infections.
VRE: Vancomycin-resistant enterococci; covered by linezolid, daptomycin, and quinupristin-dalfopristin (E. faecium only).
streptogramin: Antibiotic class (quinupristin-dalfopristin, A+B) binding the 50S subunit; covers E. faecium (incl. VRE) but NOT E. faecalis.
lefamulin: Pleuromutilin binding the 50S subunit (pocket closes around the drug); approved for community-acquired pneumonia; covers atypicals.
pleuromutilin: Antibiotic class (lefamulin) binding the 50S subunit; its pocket closes around the drug to block tRNA binding.
antifolate: Drug class blocking folate metabolism; selective because mammals ingest folate while bacteria/protozoa synthesize it from PABA. Ultimately DNA-synthesis inhibitors.
PABA: Para-aminobenzoic acid; the bacterial substrate for folate synthesis. Sulfonamides are PABA analogs inhibiting dihydropteroate synthase.
tetrahydrofolate: The active folate cofactor for purine/pyrimidine synthesis; antifolates ultimately block its production.
dihydropteroate synthase: Folate-synthesis enzyme (the PABA step) inhibited by sulfonamides.
dihydrofolate reductase: DHFR; folate-reduction enzyme inhibited by trimethoprim (bacterial), pyrimethamine/proguanil (protozoal), and methotrexate (mammalian).
DHFR: Dihydrofolate reductase; reduces dihydrofolate to active tetrahydrofolate. Trimethoprim hits bacterial DHFR; methotrexate hits mammalian.
sulfonamide: PABA-analog antibiotic competitively inhibiting dihydropteroate synthase; broad-spectrum bacteriostatic; causes Stevens-Johnson, hemolysis in G6PD deficiency, kernicterus, crystalluria.
trimethoprim: Folate-REDUCTION inhibitor of bacterial DHFR; penetrates the prostate (non-ionized); high doses cause megaloblastic anemia.
TMP-SMX: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (Bactrim/Septra): sequential folate blockade (160/800 mg). CDC first-line for UTI; drug of choice for Pneumocystis (PCP).
sulfasalazine: Poorly absorbed sulfonamide acting in the gut; niche is inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis, Crohn).
silver sulfadiazine: Topical sulfonamide preventing colonization of BURN wounds.
sulfadoxine: Long-acting sulfonamide paired with pyrimethamine (Fansidar) for mefloquine-resistant malaria.
Fansidar: Sulfadoxine + pyrimethamine: a folate-synthesis inhibitor plus a protozoal DHFR inhibitor, used for resistant malaria.
Stevens-Johnson syndrome: Severe bullous skin reaction (with dermis sloughing) that can be fatal; classic sulfonamide toxicity; stop the drug and never rechallenge.
kernicterus: Bilirubin-induced neonatal brain injury; sulfonamides cause it by displacing bilirubin from albumin.
crystalluria: Sulfonamide crystal formation in ACIDIC urine; managed by hydration and alkalinizing the urine.
G6PD: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase; deficiency causes hemolytic anemia with oxidant drugs (sulfonamides, dapsone, nitrofurantoin, primaquine, antimalarials).
leucovorin: Folinic acid; given with pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine (toxoplasmosis) to protect host bone marrow.
fluoroquinolone: Bactericidal inhibitors of DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II); '-floxacin' suffix; signature tendinopathy/tendon rupture; avoid under 18 and in pregnancy.
DNA gyrase: Bacterial topoisomerase II (subunit GyrA cuts strands); the target of fluoroquinolones.
GyrA: DNA-gyrase subunit that performs strand-cutting and is the fluoroquinolone target; point mutations in gyrA confer resistance.
ciprofloxacin: Best antipseudomonal fluoroquinolone and gram-negative workhorse; paired with vancomycin for empiric MRSA + Pseudomonas coverage.
levofloxacin: Respiratory fluoroquinolone for community-acquired pneumonia and atypicals.
moxifloxacin: Respiratory fluoroquinolone; CANNOT treat UTI because it is eliminated by the biliary route (never reaches the urine).
nalidixic acid: The original quinolone (for E. coli UTI) from which fluoroquinolones are fluorinated derivatives.
tendinopathy: Fluoroquinolone class-defining toxicity (tendon rupture), classically of the Achilles tendon.
nitrofurantoin: Unique-mechanism urinary antibiotic; avoid in pregnancy and G6PD deficiency (oxidant -> hemolysis).
methenamine: Urinary antiseptic inert at blood pH that decomposes in ACIDIC urine to bactericidal FORMALDEHYDE; chronic suppressive use only; no tissue activity.
nucleoside analog: Antiviral that is INERT until a viral or host kinase phosphorylates it; activation by a VIRAL kinase confers selectivity for infected cells.
acyclovir: Acyclic GUANOSINE analog activated by viral THYMIDINE KINASE, then inhibits viral DNA polymerase; prototype against HSV-1 and HSV-2.
thymidine kinase: Viral kinase performing the first phosphorylation that activates acyclovir, conferring selectivity for infected cells.
foscarnet: PYROPHOSPHATE analog antiviral needing NO phosphorylation; used for CMV retinitis in the immunocompromised; nephrotoxic.
vidarabine: IV nucleoside analog for HSV encephalitis.
neuraminidase: Influenza surface enzyme mediating viral EXIT; inhibited by the '-mivir' drugs (oseltamivir, zanamivir, peramivir).
hemagglutinin: Influenza surface protein mediating viral ENTRY (the 'H' in H1N1).
oseltamivir: Neuraminidase inhibitor ('-mivir') blocking influenza viral exit.
amantadine: Adamantane blocking the influenza A M2 ion channel/uncoating (CDC recommends AGAINST due to resistance); also used for parkinsonism dyskinesia.
baloxavir: Influenza drug inhibiting the cap-dependent endonuclease of the viral polymerase (blocks 'cap snatching').
M2 ion channel: Influenza A uncoating channel blocked by adamantanes (amantadine, rimantadine); resistance led the CDC to recommend against them.
NRTI: Nucleoside reverse-transcriptase inhibitor; a base analog that NEEDS phosphorylation to act against HIV reverse transcriptase.
NNRTI: Non-nucleoside reverse-transcriptase inhibitor; binds reverse transcriptase DIRECTLY (no phosphorylation) with less resistance than NRTIs.
tenofovir: Nucleotide RT inhibitor (NtRTI) already phosphorylated; used in HIV (and HBV, with entecavir) and in PrEP (emtricitabine + tenofovir).
reverse transcriptase: Viral RNA-DIRECTED DNA polymerase (reads RNA to make DNA), something mammalian cells lack; target of NRTIs/NNRTIs in HIV and used by HBV.
protease inhibitor: HIV drug class ('-navir') blocking cleavage of the Gag-Pol polyprotein, leaving virions immature and non-infectious; contraindicated with rifampin.
Gag-Pol: The HIV polyprotein whose cleavage by viral protease is blocked by protease inhibitors, keeping virions immature/non-infectious.
raltegravir: HIV INTEGRASE inhibitor ('-tegravir'); best at preventing latent integrated virus (e.g. post-needlestick).
integrase inhibitor: HIV drug class ('-tegravir', e.g. raltegravir) blocking viral genome integration; key after needlestick exposure.
PrEP: Pre-exposure prophylaxis for HIV; emtricitabine + tenofovir (Truvada/Descovy).
entecavir: Reverse-transcriptase inhibitor (with tenofovir) suppressing HBV, which replicates via an RNA intermediate.
HBV: Hepatitis B virus; a DNA virus that builds its genome through an RNA intermediate using reverse transcriptase (hence RT inhibitors work).
HCV: Hepatitis C virus; first viral disease ever CURED by drugs, using an NS3/4A protease inhibitor plus an NS5B polymerase inhibitor (sofosbuvir-based).
NS5B: HCV NS5B polymerase; inhibited (e.g. by sofosbuvir) as part of the curative HCV regimen.
NS3/4A: HCV NS3/4A protease; inhibited as part of the curative HCV combination.
remdesivir: COVID-19 antiviral inhibiting the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp).
RdRp: RNA-dependent RNA polymerase; the replication enzyme of RNA viruses (e.g. SARS-CoV-2) targeted by remdesivir.
baricitinib: JAK inhibitor used in COVID-19 to target INFLAMMATION (not the virus itself).
tocilizumab: IL-6 receptor monoclonal antibody used in COVID-19 to target inflammation.
palivizumab: IM monoclonal antibody preventing RSV infection (originally in infants, now adults too).
imiquimod: Immune-response modifier (TLR agonist inducing local interferon) for HPV warts; NOT a direct antiviral.
pentamidine: Drug for early African trypanosomiasis; also an alternative for Pneumocystis (PCP).
melarsoprol: TRIVALENT ARSENICAL for CNS-stage African trypanosomiasis; binds parasitic enzyme sulfhydryl groups.
nifurtimox: Drug for T. cruzi (Chagas / American trypanosomiasis); generates intracellular free radicals that kill the organism.
eflornithine: Inhibitor of ornithine decarboxylase; used for late-stage West African trypanosomiasis.
metronidazole: Drug of choice for giardiasis, trichomoniasis, and amebiasis; activated only in ANAEROBIC cells (acts as electron acceptor, shredding DNA); disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol.
paromomycin: Non-absorbed aminoglycoside; preferred for luminal amebiasis/giardiasis carriers and in pregnancy.
chloroquine: First-line antimalarial inhibiting plasmodial heme polymerase, so toxic free heme accumulates in the parasite.
primaquine: ONLY antimalarial that eradicates the latent liver (hypnozoite) stage of P. vivax/ovale; causes hemolysis in G6PD deficiency (screen first).
quinine: Chloroquine-resistant malaria backup; signature toxicity CINCHONISM (hearing, visual, and balance disturbance).
cinchonism: Quinine toxicity cluster of hearing, visual, and balance disturbance.
artemisinin: Antimalarial class; artemether-lumefantrine (Coartem) is the artemisinin combination for resistant falciparum malaria.
Coartem: Artemether-lumefantrine; the artemisinin-based combination for resistant falciparum malaria.
Malarone: Atovaquone-proguanil: a protozoal DHFR inhibitor (proguanil) plus a mitochondrial oxidative-phosphorylation inhibitor (atovaquone).
mebendazole: Benzimidazole anthelmintic for nematodes (roundworms); inhibits parasite microtubule synthesis so the worm is expelled.
albendazole: Benzimidazole anthelmintic for nematodes; inhibits parasite microtubule synthesis.
praziquantel: Anthelmintic for cestodes and trematodes (incl. schistosomiasis); raises membrane calcium permeability causing tetanic worm contraction.
ivermectin: Anthelmintic opening parasite chloride channels (paralysis); drug for onchocerciasis (river blindness).
diethylcarbamazine: Drug for lymphatic filariasis, targeting microfilariae rather than adult worms.
pyrimethamine: Protozoal DHFR inhibitor; with a sulfonamide (sulfadiazine) treats toxoplasmosis (plus leucovorin).
PCP: Pneumocystis pneumonia (Pneumocystis jirovecii); first-line treatment TMP-SMX; alternatives pentamidine, atovaquone, dapsone.
mab: Drug-name suffix (-mab) signaling a MONOCLONAL ANTIBODY; tested by generic, never brand, name.
monoclonal antibody: Engineered antibody drug; mechanisms include neutralization, receptor blockade, ADCC, CDC, and payload delivery.
receptor blockade: mAb mechanism: the antibody sits on a cell-surface receptor so the ligand cannot bind or signal.
CDC: Complement-Dependent Cytotoxicity; an mAb activates complement, leading to cell lysis. (Note: 'CDC' also denotes the public-health agency on some guideline cards.)
payload delivery: mAb mechanism: conjugating the antibody to a toxin or radioactive isotope for targeted cytotoxicity.
dupilumab: mAb blocking IL-4 and IL-13 signaling to treat atopic dermatitis (eczema).
lecanemab: Anti-amyloid-beta monoclonal antibody used in early Alzheimer disease.
donanemab: Anti-amyloid-beta monoclonal antibody used in early Alzheimer disease.
amyloid-beta: The protein targeted by anti-amyloid mAbs (lecanemab, donanemab) in early Alzheimer disease.
bispecific: Antibody with two arms binding two antigens at once, classically bridging a cancer cell to a T cell (e.g. blinatumomab).
blinatumomab: Bispecific antibody bridging CD19 on the cancer B cell and CD3 on the T cell.
cytokine-release syndrome: Signature toxicity of CAR-T therapy; a systemic inflammatory cytokine surge.
ASO: Antisense oligonucleotide; single-strand DNA/RNA binding mRNA to block translation or trigger degradation; works in both nucleus and cytoplasm.
siRNA: Small interfering RNA; double-stranded RNA using the RISC complex to degrade a spliced mRNA; acts in the cytoplasm only.
RISC: RNA-induced silencing complex; the machinery siRNA uses to degrade target mRNA.
AAV: Adeno-associated virus; the usual gene-therapy vector that does NOT integrate into the genome (safer than lentivirus).
lentivirus: An integrating gene-therapy vector; contrasted with AAV, which does not integrate.
CRISPR: CRISPR-Cas9; makes a precise edit to the patient's DNA. First approved therapy is Casgevy for sickle cell disease.
Casgevy: First approved CRISPR therapy, for sickle cell disease; disrupts BCL11A to raise fetal hemoglobin.
mRNA: Messenger RNA therapy delivering synthetic mRNA so the cell translates a protein/antigen; the model for the COVID-19 vaccine spike protein.
superinfection: Overgrowth (classically Candida) when a broad-spectrum antibiotic disrupts normal flora.
antibiogram: Institution/unit-specific susceptibility pattern used to guide empiric antibiotic choice.
bacteriostatic: Drug that arrests bacterial growth so the immune system clears the organism; can blunt a bactericidal drug (antagonism).
bactericidal: Drug that KILLS bacteria outright; favored in immunocompromised patients.
concentration-dependent: Killing that increases with peak drug level (aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones); dosed as large doses at long intervals.
time-dependent: Killing that depends on time above MIC (beta-lactams); dosed frequently to keep levels above MIC.
MIC: Minimum inhibitory concentration; the level a time-dependent antibiotic must stay above between doses.
synergy: Combined effect greater than additive (e.g. beta-lactam + aminoglycoside; sequential folate blockade); also slows resistance.
efflux: Resistance mechanism pumping drug back out of the cell; notorious for tetracyclines.
ergosterol: The fungal membrane sterol that is the master antifungal target: polyenes BIND it, azoles and terbinafine BLOCK its synthesis.
amphotericin B: Polyene that BINDS ergosterol and forms membrane pores; fungicidal and broadest-spectrum antifungal; dose-limiting nephrotoxicity plus infusion reactions.
nystatin: Polyene used TOPICALLY only (oral thrush, cutaneous/vaginal Candida) because it is too toxic systemically.
flucytosine: Antifungal converted by fungal cytosine deaminase into 5-FU (inhibits thymidylate synthase); combined with amphotericin B; signature reversible bone-marrow suppression.
5-fluorouracil: 5-FU; the active product flucytosine is converted into by fungal cytosine deaminase, inhibiting thymidylate synthase.
azole: Antifungal class inhibiting 14-alpha-demethylase (blocks lanosterol -> ergosterol), fungistatic; also inhibits human CYP (many drug interactions).
14-alpha-demethylase: Fungal P450 enzyme inhibited by azoles, blocking conversion of lanosterol to ergosterol.
ketoconazole: Imidazole antifungal that also blocks steroidogenesis (gynecomastia) and is hepatotoxic; also a potent CYP inhibitor.
fluconazole: Azole with excellent CSF penetration; used for cryptococcal meningitis.
voriconazole: Azole that is first-line for invasive aspergillosis.
griseofulvin: Antifungal binding microtubules (disrupts mitotic spindle); deposits in keratin, treating DERMATOPHYTES only; requires long therapy.
echinocandin: Antifungal class (the '-fungins') inhibiting beta-1,3-glucan synthase (fungal CELL WALL); very safe (humans lack a cell wall); fungicidal vs Candida.
beta-1,3-glucan synthase: Fungal cell-wall enzyme inhibited by echinocandins; humans lack this target, making echinocandins very safe.
terbinafine: Allylamine inhibiting squalene epoxidase (depletes ergosterol, builds toxic squalene); oral drug of choice for onychomycosis.
squalene epoxidase: Ergosterol-synthesis enzyme inhibited by terbinafine, depleting ergosterol and accumulating toxic squalene.
dermatophyte: Keratin-loving fungus (tinea); treated by griseofulvin and terbinafine.
onychomycosis: Fungal nail infection; terbinafine is the oral drug of choice.
graded: Dose-response curve plotting magnitude of effect in one system (vs quantal, which plots fraction of a population responding).
quantal: Dose-response curve plotting the FRACTION of a population responding (vs graded magnitude).
WARNING: Mnemonic for narrow-therapeutic-index drugs needing monitoring: Warfarin, Theophylline, Digoxin, Anti-epileptics, Lithium.
warfarin: Highly protein-bound, narrow-TI anticoagulant; FIRST-order kinetics (the slide wrongly listed it as zero-order). Free level/INR raised by CYP inhibitors and by albumin displacement (e.g. sulfadiazine).
phenytoin: Antiepileptic with ZERO-order kinetics at therapeutic doses; highly protein-bound; level raised by chloramphenicol (CYP inhibition).
SVT: Supraventricular tachycardia; driven by RIGHT-sided (SA node) hypersympathetic activity. A right pectoralis major trigger point is a listed driver.
EPS: Extrapyramidal symptoms (antipsychotic-induced acute dystonia); treated acutely with antimuscarinics like benztropine.
serotonin syndrome: Risk when linezolid (a weak MAO inhibitor) is combined with serotonergic drugs.
miosis: Pupil constriction from parasympathetic/muscarinic (M3) iris-sphincter contraction; produced by cholinergic glaucoma drugs.
mydriasis: Pupil dilation from antimuscarinic block of the iris sphincter; can raise IOP and precipitate angle-closure glaucoma.
cycloplegia: Paralysis of accommodation (ciliary muscle); phenylephrine gives mydriasis WITHOUT cycloplegia, unlike antimuscarinics.
IOP: Intraocular pressure; raised by antimuscarinic mydriasis (cutting aqueous outflow) in narrow-angle glaucoma.
orthostatic hypotension: Postural drop in blood pressure; classic first-dose effect of prazosin/terazosin/doxazosin; additive with tricyclic antidepressants.
IFIS: Intraoperative floppy iris syndrome; an alpha-1-blocker adverse effect, most pronounced with tamsulosin; flag '-osin' use before cataract surgery.
rebound hypertension: Surge in blood pressure on abruptly stopping a central alpha-2 agonist like clonidine.
pheochromocytoma: Catecholamine-secreting tumor; treat with an ALPHA-blocker FIRST (phenoxybenzamine pre-op) before any beta-blocker to avoid unopposed alpha vasoconstriction.
TCA: Tricyclic antidepressant; potentiates NE/epi by blocking reuptake; overdose with widening QRS treated with sodium bicarbonate; additive orthostatic hypotension with alpha-blockers.
sodium bicarbonate: Alkalinizes urine to trap weak-acid overdoses (phenobarbital, methotrexate, aspirin); in TCA overdose given FIRST to treat cardiac Na-channel toxicity (widening QRS).
ammonium chloride: Acidifies urine to trap weak-base overdoses (TCAs, amphetamines) for excretion.
Listeria: Gram-positive rod; ampicillin is the drug of choice.
Candida: Yeast causing thrush and superinfection; echinocandins are first-line (fungicidal) for invasive candidiasis; nystatin topical for thrush.
aspergillosis: Invasive mold infection; voriconazole is first-line.
cryptococcal meningitis: Cryptococcus CNS infection; treated with flucytosine + amphotericin B; fluconazole penetrates CSF.
Lyme disease: Tick-borne Borrelia infection; doxycycline is first-line.
Rocky Mountain spotted fever: Rickettsial tick-borne illness; doxycycline is first-line.
community-acquired pneumonia: CAP; first-line azithromycin (with amoxicillin/doxycycline alternatives); respiratory fluoroquinolones and lefamulin also used.
hepatotoxicity: Liver injury; a signature toxicity of isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ketoconazole, labetalol, and (withdrawn) trovafloxacin.
peripheral neuropathy: Nerve damage; signature isoniazid toxicity (prevented by pyridoxine), worse in slow acetylators.
hemolytic anemia: Oxidant-drug-induced RBC destruction in G6PD deficiency (sulfonamides, dapsone, nitrofurantoin, primaquine).
QT prolongation: Cardiac repolarization delay risking torsades; caused by macrolides, certain fluoroquinolones, alfuzosin.
torsades: Torsades de pointes; polymorphic VT precipitated by QT-prolonging drugs (e.g. withdrawn fluoroquinolones).
disulfiram-like: Acetaldehyde-accumulation reaction (flushing, nausea) with alcohol; caused by metronidazole and MTT-side-chain cephalosporins (blocking aldehyde dehydrogenase).
aldehyde dehydrogenase: Enzyme blocked in disulfiram-like reactions (metronidazole, MTT cephalosporins), causing acetaldehyde buildup with alcohol.
hyperuricemia: Elevated uric acid (gout/joint pain); a signature pyrazinamide toxicity.
retrobulbar optic neuritis: Ethambutol's signature ocular toxicity, with red-green color blindness.
P. falciparum: The malignant, severe malaria species (no dormant liver stage).
T. cruzi: Trypanosoma cruzi; cause of Chagas disease (American trypanosomiasis) with cardiomyopathy and megacolon; treated with nifurtimox.
amebiasis: Entamoeba infection; treated with metronidazole (tissue) and paromomycin (luminal carriers).
giardiasis: Giardia infection; treated with metronidazole (or paromomycin in pregnancy).
AIDS: Advanced HIV; setting for PCP prophylaxis (dapsone/TMP-SMX) and disseminated MAC infection.
neuropraxia: MILDEST grade of nerve injury: damages only the MYELIN, with axon and connective tissue intact. Fully recovers once remyelination occurs.
axonotmesis: Intermediate nerve injury: myelin AND axon break down (Wallerian degeneration) but the CONNECTIVE-TISSUE SHEATH stays intact, so the axon CAN regrow along the preserved tube.
neurotmesis: MOST SEVERE nerve injury: severs myelin, axon, AND connective tissue, so there is NO regrowth without surgical repair.
Wallerian degeneration: Breakdown of the axon and myelin distal to a nerve injury (seen in axonotmesis and neurotmesis); a preserved connective-tissue sheath is what allows subsequent regrowth.
myelin: Insulating sheath around an axon; the ONLY element damaged in the mildest nerve injury (neuropraxia), which is why that grade fully recovers.
connective-tissue sheath: The endoneurial tube surrounding an axon; if INTACT (as in axonotmesis) it guides axonal regrowth, but if severed (neurotmesis) there is no regrowth.
NCS/EMG: Nerve conduction studies / electromyography: the BEST test to confirm and grade a nerve entrapment and to separate a PERIPHERAL lesion from a central (radiculopathy) one.
needle EMG/NCS: Needle electromyography with nerve conduction studies: the GOLD-STANDARD diagnostic for radiculopathy and the only tool that assesses the PHYSIOLOGICAL INTEGRITY of nerve roots and localizes the lesion.
entrapment neuropathy: Focal nerve compression at a discrete anatomic site, producing deficits LOCALIZED to or distal to the compression (unlike radiculopathy, which spans the whole dermatome).
median nerve: Most common entrapment neuropathy of the UPPER EXTREMITY; its compression at the wrist causes carpal tunnel syndrome.
carpal tunnel: Median nerve entrapment at the WRIST (under the flexor retinaculum); SPARES thenar sensation because the palmar cutaneous branch leaves before the retinaculum.
thenar: The thumb-side palmar muscle bulk; its SENSATION is SPARED in carpal tunnel because the palmar cutaneous branch departs before the flexor retinaculum (numb thenar instead implicates a proximal/pronator-teres lesion).
palmar cutaneous: Branch of the median nerve to the thenar skin that leaves BEFORE the flexor retinaculum, so a wrist (carpal tunnel) lesion SPARES thenar sensation.
pronator teres: Proximal forearm site of median nerve entrapment; a lesion here (unlike carpal tunnel) involves the thenar pad because it is proximal to the palmar cutaneous branch.
AIN syndrome: Anterior interosseous nerve syndrome: a PURE MOTOR median branch lesion; patient cannot make a rounded 'O' (pinch) with thumb and index, with NO sensory loss.
suprascapular nerve: Nerve at risk in the shoulder; compression at the suprascapular notch loses abduction AND external rotation, while compression at the spinoglenoid notch loses external rotation ONLY.
suprascapular notch: Proximal suprascapular nerve compression site; entrapment here loses BOTH abduction and external rotation (supraspinatus + infraspinatus).
spinoglenoid notch: Distal suprascapular nerve compression site; entrapment here loses external rotation ONLY (infraspinatus), sparing abduction.
Froment: Ulnar-nerve sign: the patient flexes the thumb IP joint (recruiting FPL via the median nerve) to pinch a paper because adductor pollicis is weak.
Wartenberg: Ulnar-nerve sign: persistently ABDUCTED little finger from unopposed extensor digiti minimi against a weak palmar interosseous.
claw hand: Ulnar-nerve deformity: hyperextended MCP and flexed IP joints of the 4th and 5th digits from intrinsic muscle weakness.
radial nerve: Nerve injured at the spiral groove ('Saturday night palsy'), causing WRIST DROP plus dorsal-hand sensory loss.
spiral groove: Humeral site of radial nerve compression ('Saturday night palsy'); injury causes wrist drop with dorsal-hand sensory loss.
wrist drop: Inability to extend the wrist from a RADIAL nerve injury at the spiral groove ('Saturday night palsy'), with dorsal-hand sensory loss.
PIN: Posterior interosseous nerve (deep radial branch); entrapment is PURE MOTOR causing FINGER DROP with NO sensory loss, and spares the ECRL (so wrist extension is preserved).
finger drop: Inability to extend the fingers at the MCP joints from a posterior interosseous nerve (PIN) lesion; pure motor with no sensory loss.
ECRL: Extensor carpi radialis longus; SPARED in posterior interosseous nerve (PIN) palsy, so wrist extension persists even with finger drop.
common peroneal nerve: Nerve at the fibular head; the MOST COMMON mononeuropathy of the LOWER EXTREMITY, causing FOOT DROP.
foot drop: Inability to dorsiflex the foot, classically from common peroneal nerve injury at the fibular head; present at INITIAL evaluation it signals a POOR prognosis.
deep peroneal: Branch giving DORSIFLEXION and FIRST-WEB-SPACE sensation; lost in deep peroneal entrapment.
superficial peroneal: Branch giving foot EVERSION and sensation over the rest of the dorsum of the foot.
sciatic nerve: Nerve carrying the peroneal division; at risk after HIP operations (always check for foot drop) and entrapped in piriformis syndrome.
piriformis syndrome: Sciatic irritation by the piriformis: buttock/posterior-thigh pain WORSE after prolonged sitting, an external-rotation preference, and a positive FAIR test; pain usually does NOT go past the knee.
FAIR: Flexion-Adduction-Internal-Rotation test: provocative maneuver POSITIVE in piriformis syndrome (stretches the piriformis and compresses the sciatic nerve).
hamstring syndrome: Triad of pain IMMEDIATELY on sitting, pain on resisted knee flexion at 90 degrees of hip flexion, and ischial-tuberosity tenderness.
meralgia paresthetica: Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve entrapment; PURELY SENSORY (anterolateral thigh), so the EMG is NORMAL.
lateral femoral cutaneous nerve: Purely sensory nerve to the anterolateral thigh; its entrapment is meralgia paresthetica, with a NORMAL EMG.
true rib: Ribs 1-7; reach the sternum by their OWN costal cartilage. Also called VERTEBROSTERNAL ribs.
vertebrosternal: Attachment-based name for a TRUE rib (ribs 1-7), which connects to the sternum by its own costal cartilage.
false rib: Ribs 8-10; their cartilage attaches to THE RIB ABOVE rather than directly to the sternum. Also called VERTEBROCHONDRAL ribs.
vertebrochondral: Attachment-based name for a FALSE rib (ribs 8-10), whose cartilage joins the rib above instead of the sternum.
floating rib: Ribs 11-12; have NO ANTERIOR attachment and end in the posterior abdominal musculature.
typical rib: Ribs 3-9 (by SHAPE): articulate with TWO vertebrae and have a head, neck, tubercle, body, and costal angle. Shape and attachment are independent axes (e.g. rib 8 is typical AND false).
atypical rib: Ribs 1, 2, 10, 11, and 12 (by SHAPE), lacking the full typical landmark set or two-vertebra articulation.
tubercle: Posterior rib landmark that forms the costotransverse joint with the vertebral transverse process; part of the typical-rib landmark set.
costotransverse joint: Articulation between a rib tubercle and a vertebral transverse process; ABSENT on ribs 11-12, which is why caliper ribs move both AP and transverse.
sympathetic chain: Paired chain of ganglia lying ANTERIOR to the rib heads in SHARED FASCIA; a restricted rib stresses that fascia and raises sympathetic tone (rib-raising frees it).
shared fascia: Connective tissue linking the rib heads to the sympathetic chain ganglia; rib restriction stresses it and increases sympathetic tone.
rib-raising: OMT that frees the costovertebral/shared fascia to normalize sympathetic regulation; LONG application (>90 s) DECREASES sympathetics (pneumonia), SHORT bursts STIMULATE them (acute asthma).
diaphragm: PRIMARY muscle of respiration, generating ~60% of inspiratory pressure change; on inhalation it CONTRACTS and descends inferiorly. Driven by the phrenic nerve (C3-C5).
pump-handle: Rib motion (ribs 2-5) that raises the anterior end and increases the ANTERIOR-POSTERIOR (AP) diameter; rotates on a TRANSVERSE axis; palpated parasternally; sharp/pinprick pain.
bucket-handle: Rib motion (ribs 6-10) that raises the lateral edge and increases the TRANSVERSE diameter; rotates on an AP axis; palpated at the mid-axillary line; deep, dull, aching pain.
caliper: Rib motion (ribs 11-12) that increases BOTH AP and transverse diameters slightly because these ribs have NO costotransverse joint.
mid-axillary line: Palpation/pain site for BUCKET-HANDLE ribs (the lateral edge), where deep dull aching motion is assessed.
inhaled rib: Rib SD that rises easily with inhalation but won't recede on exhalation (lives in inhalation); on exam the space below it widens. Pain ON exhalation suggests an inhaled rib.
exhaled rib: Rib SD that moves into exhalation but won't rise on inhalation (lives in exhalation). Pain ON inhalation suggests an exhaled rib. A rib SD is named for its position of EASE.
scalene: Accessory respiratory and cervical muscle group: anterior/middle scalenes elevate rib 1 and the posterior scalene elevates rib 2; acting unilaterally they sidebend the neck IPSILATERALLY, bilaterally they flex it. Tightness can compress the lower brachial plexus.
anterior scalene: With the middle scalene, attaches to and elevates RIB 1; a tight scalene can compress the lower brachial plexus (thoracic outlet symptoms in digits 4-5).
posterior scalene: Scalene that attaches to and elevates RIB 2 as an accessory muscle of inhalation.
pectoralis minor: Muscle treated in rib-dance ME for exhaled pump ribs 3-5; also an anterior thoracic-outlet compressor.
serratus anterior: Muscle addressed in rib-dance ME for exhaled pump ribs 6-10.
Rib-group treatment rule: treat the BOTTOM rib first for an INHALED group; treat the TOP rib first for an EXHALED group.
Tietze: Costochondral-junction pain syndrome distinguished from costochondritis by visible SWELLING/EDEMA at the joint.
costochondritis: Tender costochondral junction WITHOUT visible swelling; adding visible swelling/edema upgrades the label to Tietze syndrome.
cervical rib: Supernumerary rib that compresses the LOWER TRUNK of the brachial plexus, producing thoracic outlet syndrome.
thoracic outlet syndrome: Compression of the brachial plexus/vessels at the thoracic outlet (e.g. by a cervical rib or tight scalenes), classically affecting the lower trunk and digits 4-5.
herpes zoster: Shingles: reactivation of varicella in the DORSAL ROOT GANGLION causing deep BURNING, DERMATOMAL pain on ONE side.
dorsal root ganglion: Sensory ganglion housing the cell bodies of primary afferents; site of varicella reactivation in herpes zoster (shingles).
scapular dyskinesis: 'Sick scapula': confirmed by the scapular repositioning test (retract/stabilize the scapula and repeat painful flexion); if pain resolves, treat the scapular STABILIZERS, not the rotator cuff.
CRPS: Complex regional pain syndrome: a CLINICAL (Budapest) diagnosis of regional pain that is DISPROPORTIONATE, NON-DERMATOMAL, and DISTAL-predominant, with NO confirmatory lab or imaging test. Type I has no nerve lesion; Type II has a confirmed peripheral nerve lesion.
CRPS Type I: Disproportionate regional pain with NO confirmed peripheral nerve lesion (formerly reflex sympathetic dystrophy).
CRPS Type II: Same CRPS picture but WITH a confirmed peripheral nerve lesion (formerly causalgia); the nerve lesion is the single feature separating it from Type I.
Budapest: The clinical diagnostic criteria for CRPS; CRPS is a CLINICAL diagnosis with NO confirmatory lab or imaging test.
Allodynia: Pain from a stimulus that is NOT normally painful (a sock, a feather); a hallmark of central sensitization in CRPS.
Hyperalgesia: Abnormally HIGH pain from a stimulus that WOULD normally hurt; a sensory feature of CRPS/central sensitization.
central sensitization: Amplified pain processing: NMDA-driven WIND-UP plus receptive-field EXPANSION plus loss of GABA/glycine inhibition.
wind-up: Progressive increase in dorsal-horn neuron response to repeated C-fiber input; an NMDA-driven component of central sensitization.
NMDA antagonist: Drug class (e.g. KETAMINE) that blocks the NMDA receptor to dampen central sensitization/wind-up; used in refractory CRPS.
ketamine: An NMDA ANTAGONIST used for refractory CRPS; dampens central sensitization/wind-up.
GABA/glycine: The main INHIBITORY neurotransmitters of the dorsal horn; LOSS of their inhibition contributes to central sensitization.
livedo reticularis: Lace-like purplish mottled skin from arteriolar vasospasm pooling deoxygenated blood in the subpapillary venous plexus; a sign of CRPS Stage 3.
osteoporosis: Reduced bone density; appears patchy in CRPS Stage 2 and makes HVLA risky (favor indirect techniques) in CRPS OMT.
stellate ganglion: Cervicothoracic sympathetic ganglion; a sympathetic block here that relieves pain is a POSITIVE CRPS test, but a NEGATIVE block does NOT rule out CRPS.
