HVLA: High-velocity, low-amplitude thrust technique; used with CAUTION (or avoided) where bone is fragile (CRPS osteoporosis) and in the radiculopathy region.
intrinsic: Deep cervical muscles near the axis of rotation that give PRECISE SEGMENTAL control.
extrinsic: Cervical muscles far from the axis of rotation that provide POWER, not precise control.
articular pillar: The bony column of the cervical facets; PALPATED and TRANSLATED to diagnose the cervical spine (NOT the transverse processes).
translation: Side-to-side gliding of a cervical segment used in motion testing; translating the pillar to one side induces sidebending to the OPPOSITE side, so limited RIGHT translation means restricted LEFT sidebending (the segment lives in right sidebending).
Fryette's principles: Spinal coupling rules; the CERVICAL spine does NOT follow Fryette's principles 1 and 2, instead using three modified region-specific rules.
myodural bridge: Connective-tissue connection from rectus capitis posterior minor to the intracranial DURA; tension here generates cervicogenic headache.
rectus capitis posterior minor: Suboccipital muscle linked to the intracranial dura by the myodural bridge; the most-midline finger targets it in the OAD-compression headache hold.
dura: Outermost meningeal layer; tethered to rectus capitis posterior minor via the myodural bridge, a source of cervicogenic headache.
SCM: Sternocleidomastoid: acting unilaterally it sidebends IPSILATERALLY but rotates CONTRALATERALLY; an accessory respiratory muscle whose use at rest signals increased work of breathing.
BUM: Cervical facet orientation: superior facets face Backward, Upward, MEDIAL.
BUL: Thoracic facet orientation: superior facets face Backward, Upward, LATERAL.
radiculopathy: Disease of the spinal nerve ROOTS; a pure LOWER-MOTOR-NEURON problem with deficits along the ENTIRE dermatome, pain worst proximally and paresthesias worst distally, worsened by cough/Valsalva.
cervical spondylosis: Degenerative bony spurring of the cervical spine; a compressive cause of cervical radiculopathy.
spinal stenosis: Narrowing of the spinal canal or foramina; a compressive cause of cervical radiculopathy.
Valsalva: Forced expiration against a closed glottis; WORSENS radicular symptoms with a herniation/mass by raising intraspinal pressure.
Spurling: Cervical compression test that WORSENS radicular symptoms because axial load narrows the neural foramen; a negative does NOT rule out foraminal stenosis.
distraction: Cervical traction that IMPROVES radicular symptoms by opening the neural foramen.
clonus: Rhythmic involuntary muscle contractions; corresponds to reflex grade 4 and is ALWAYS abnormal (an upper-motor-neuron sign).
Lhermitte: Shock-like paresthesia down the spine/limbs triggered by NECK FLEXION; a sign of cervical cord pathology.
Hoffmann: Flicking the middle-finger nail produces reflex flexion of the index and thumb; an UPPER-MOTOR-NEURON sign (upper-limb analog of Babinski) and a myelopathy red flag.
myelopathy: Spinal-CORD dysfunction giving a MIXED UMN/LMN picture: hyporeflexia AT the lesion level and hyperreflexia BELOW it, with long-tract signs (gait ataxia, hand clumsiness).
Cervical spondylotic myelopathy: Most common cause of spinal-cord dysfunction in the ELDERLY; a BROAD-BASED gait may be the presenting sign.
lower-motor-neuron: Motor neuron from the anterior horn to muscle; radiculopathy is a PURE LMN problem (weakness, hyporeflexia, atrophy).
upper-motor-neuron: Motor neuron of the corticospinal tract; its signs (hyperreflexia, clonus, Hoffmann, broad-based gait) indicate myelopathy.
anterior C7: Anterior cervical 7 tender point; counterstrain treatment position is FLEX, sidebend TOWARD, rotate AWAY.
counterstrain: Indirect OMT that places a tender point into a position of EASE (e.g. anterior C7: flex, sidebend toward, rotate away) and holds.
vagus: Cranial nerve X providing PARASYMPATHETIC supply to the lungs (bronchoconstriction + thinned secretions) and heart (slows rate/contractility); its tone is modulated at the OA/C2-C3/cranial base.
vagus nerve: Cranial nerve X (CN X): the PARASYMPATHETIC supply to the thoracic and abdominal viscera; treat the OA, C2-C3, and cranial base to normalize its tone.
bronchodilation: Airway widening produced by SYMPATHETIC (T2-T7) activity; the desired effect in acute asthma, achieved with short bursts of rib-raising.
bronchoconstriction: Airway narrowing produced by PARASYMPATHETIC (vagal) activity, which also thins secretions.
Chapman: Chapman reflex point: a viscerosomatic fascial point whose treatment ALWAYS DECREASES sympathetic activity to the related viscus (e.g. adrenal points in HTN lower BP and aldosterone).
right lymphatic duct: Drains most of the lungs (including part of the LEFT lung), the right upper body, and right head/neck into the venous system.
lymphatic pump: OMT technique augmenting lymph return; lowers lung bacterial colony counts and shortens IV-antibiotic duration, but withheld until the patient is AFEBRILE.
Hering-Breuer: Pulmonary stretch reflex that LIMITS inspiratory depth (shallow breathing); in pneumonia it cannot distinguish air- from fluid-filled alveoli, so the congested lung trips it early.
carotid body: Peripheral chemoreceptor that DRIVES RESPIRATORY RATE UP (rapid breathing) in pneumonia in response to hypoxemia.
phrenic nerve: Nerve (C3, C4, C5) that drives the diaphragm; diaphragmatic stress therefore refers to the lower six ribs and the thoracolumbar junction.
MOPSE: Trial showing OMT plus antibiotics beat antibiotics alone in pneumonia on four endpoints: length of stay, IV-antibiotic duration, respiratory failure (ventilator), and mortality.
thoracic inlet: The lymphatic drainage OUTLET; OPENED FIRST in any lymphatic treatment before pumping fluid toward it.
viscerosomatic: Reflex linking a viscus to its spinal sympathetic level (e.g. foregut T5-T9, midgut T10-T11, hindgut T12-L2); used to localize and treat visceral dysfunction via OMT.
foregut: Embryologic gut division with viscerosomatic (sympathetic) levels T5-T9.
midgut: Embryologic gut division with viscerosomatic (sympathetic) levels T10-T11.
hindgut: Embryologic gut division with viscerosomatic (sympathetic) levels T12-L2, relaying via the LEAST splanchnic nerve and IMA ganglion; parasympathetics come from the pelvic splanchnics.
least splanchnic: Sympathetic splanchnic nerve relaying the HINDGUT (T12-L2) to the inferior mesenteric artery (IMA) ganglion.
pelvic splanchnic: Parasympathetic nerves from S2-S4 supplying the pelvic and hindgut organs (NOT the vagus).
adrenal: Gland with viscerosomatic level T10; treating its posterior Chapman points in HTN lowers BP and serum aldosterone.
aldosterone: Adrenal mineralocorticoid driving salt/water retention; serum levels FALL when adrenal Chapman points are treated in HTN.
SA node: Sinoatrial node (the pacemaker); reached by RIGHT-sided autonomic fibers. Right hypersympathetic tone drives SVTs; right hyperparasympathetic tone causes sinus bradyarrhythmias.
AV node: Atrioventricular node; reached by LEFT-sided autonomic fibers. Left hypersympathetic tone drives ectopic foci/VF; left hyperparasympathetic tone causes AV blocks.
coronary vasospasm: Sustained high cardiac sympathetic tone can produce coronary artery spasm, causing ischemia EVEN WITHOUT a fixed stenosis.
collateral circulation: Backup vascular channels; impaired cardiac lymphatic drainage REDUCES it and congests tissue, and upper-thoracic sympathetic calming removes factors that discourage it.
effleurage: Gentle stroking lymphatic technique used in CHF OMT to aid lymphatic return.
ASIS: Anterior superior iliac spine: pelvic landmark used to name innominate dysfunction (anterior rotation = ASIS inferior; inflare = ASIS toward midline; outflare = ASIS away from midline).
PSIS: Posterior superior iliac spine; on the STANDING flexion test the side whose PSIS moves MORE marks the dysfunctional (locked) SI joint.
standing flexion test: Pelvic screen for ILIOSACRAL (innominate) dysfunction; positive on the side whose PSIS moves MORE/farther superior.
seated flexion test: Pelvic screen for SACROILIAC dysfunction; positive on the side OPPOSITE the engaged oblique axis.
anterior innominate: Innominate rotated forward: ASIS INFERIOR and PSIS SUPERIOR on that side; treated by contracting the hip extensors (glut max + hamstrings).
posterior innominate: Innominate rotated backward (the reverse of anterior): ASIS superior and PSIS inferior; treated by contracting the hip flexors (quads + psoas).
superior shear: Innominate upslip: ALL landmarks SUPERIOR on that side (no up/down split, unlike a rotation).
inflare: Innominate dysfunction with the ASIS CLOSER TO (toward) midline; treated with the ADDUCTORS.
outflare: Innominate dysfunction with the ASIS FARTHER FROM midline; treated with the ABDUCTORS.
superior transverse: The S1 (superior transverse) sacral axis: the RESPIRATORY axis, synchronous with the cranial mechanism.
nutation: Sacral base moving ANTERIOR (occurs on exhalation); the opposite of counternutation.
counternutation: Sacral base moving POSTERIOR (occurs on inhalation, apex anterior); the opposite of nutation.
oblique axis: Diagonal sacral axis engaged in torsions; the seated flexion test is positive OPPOSITE the engaged oblique axis, and L5 sidebends TOWARD it.
torsion: Sacral dysfunction about an oblique axis with ILAs LESS than one thumb-width apart; forward torsions give a NEGATIVE lumbar spring and a more-symmetric sphinx, backward torsions a positive spring.
unilateral sacral: Unilateral sacral shear: ILAs MORE than one thumb-width apart on the dysfunctional side (vs a torsion, where they are less than a thumb-width apart).
lumbar spring: Sacral test pressing on the lumbosacral junction; NEGATIVE in forward torsions (springs freely) and POSITIVE in backward torsions.
sphinx: Backward-bending (prone press-up) sacral test; in FORWARD torsions the sacral bases become MORE SYMMETRICAL, in backward torsions more asymmetric.
ILA: Inferior lateral angle of the sacrum; the spacing of the two ILAs distinguishes a torsion (<1 thumb-width apart) from a unilateral shear (>1 thumb-width apart).
Fryette Type I: Neutral mechanics: sidebending and rotation couple to OPPOSITE sides, in a GROUP of 3+ segments, improving in neutral.
Fryette Type II: Flexion/extension (non-neutral) mechanics: sidebending and rotation couple to the SAME side, usually a SINGLE segment, worsening in neutral.
somatic dysfunction: Impaired function of related body-framework components; ALWAYS named for the direction of EASE / FREER motion, not the restriction.
piriformis: External hip rotator (internal rotator past 90 degrees hip flexion); origin anterolateral sacrum (S2-S4), insertion greater trochanter. A right hypertonic piriformis rotates the sacrum LEFT (a left torsion) and L5 then rotates right.
greater trochanter: Lateral femoral prominence; the INSERTION of the piriformis.
psoas major: Hip flexor; origin = TPs of T12-L5 plus bodies/discs of L1-L5, insertion = LESSER trochanter, innervation L1-L2 (+/-L3). Its dysfunction underlies psoas syndrome.
lesser trochanter: Medial femoral prominence; the INSERTION of the psoas major.
psoas syndrome: Hip-flexor dysfunction whose key (maintaining) lesion is a FLEXED L1/L2 segment; posture leans forward and to one side with lost lordosis, a positive Thomas test, an S-curve, and pelvis shifting AWAY from the tight psoas. Pain refers to the CONTRALATERAL knee and stops there.
Thomas: Test for hip-flexor (psoas) tightness; POSITIVE in psoas syndrome (the thigh won't fully extend when the opposite hip is flexed).
S-curve: Lumbar compensatory pattern in full psoas syndrome: L1/L2 Type II toward the tight side and L3-L4 Type I to the opposite side.
